House again in committee on Bill (No. 192) to enable the city of Winnipeg to utilize the Assiniboine river water-power.-Mr. Puttee.
Mr.. DEPUTY SPEAKER. The committee were considering section 4 :
The city, or its assignees, or appointees as aforesaid, may excavate, construct, operate, keep in repair and enlarge a canal (with locks, if necessary) to connect the Assiniboine river with Lake Manitoba.
-with Mr. LaRiviere's amendment thereto to strike out the words 'if necessary.'
Mr. LaRIVIERE. I am of the opinion that the canal should not be built without locks. But I want it to be provided that all works constructed under this Act must have the approval of the Governor General in Council. I am willing with a proviso to enlarge the amendment that I have suggested, and I will move that all the words in brackets, ' with locks, if necessary ' be struck out. After consultation with the promoter of the Bill, he has agreed to allow me to move that amendment; then it will remain with the Governor General in Council, as provided in clause 6, to decide whether the locks are necessary or not, and to approve of the plans for the construction of the canal. If this section 4 is left as it

is, there is nothing to provide who shall decide as to the necessity of those locks, but by striking out these four words in this clause, it remains entirely in the discretion of the Governor General in Council to decide whether there shall be locks or not. I, therefore, move that the words between brackets in the third line be struck out.

That amendment is agreeable to *ie as a matter of arrangement. I may say that the Minister of Public Works has suggested to put at the bottom of the clause ' subject to the approval of the plans by the Department of Public Works.' That would thoroughly safeguard the matter.

Amendment agreed to.
On section 5,
For the purposes aforesaid, the city or its assignees or appointees, as aforesaid may acquire lands by purchase, lease or expropriation, and for the latter purpose all the provisions of the Railway Act which relate to expropriation shall, so far as they are applicable, apply to the undertaking and works hereby authorized.

It is a little unusual to give such wide powers as these to a private company, that is to say, the powers of expropriation that are contained in the Railway Act. Along the Red river, as most gentlemen understand, and along the Assin-Iboine also, the lands fronting on the river are in small narrow lines three or four chains wide, and extending back two or four miles. They are the lands of the original settlers who came there years ago. The part on the river is the most valuable. Their homes are there, their houses are there, and their cultivation is generally there. But unless this clause is properly worded it might happen that witnesses would go into court and swear that the land was only worth $10 or $15 an acre, whereas a small portion on the river, four or five acres, would be worth $100 an acre. The house may have only an actual value of $50, whereas the land upon which it is situated and in the immediate vicinity, may be worth $500. I think this section is a little too wide, and I don't believe they should have this power under the Dominion Railway Act. As I have already pointed out, this matter is one of gigantic importance, if the company were to construct this canal, as any gentleman will see who looks at the map from an engineering point of view and understands the quantity of water that is likely to flow down into the Assiniboine river through this canal. The clause should be restricted very much, and when we get to the other clauses, I shall raise certain objections to them. I would ask the Minister of Public Works to give us his views on this entire Bill, more especially on this particular clause.

I would suggest
to the hon. gentleman in charge of this Bill that it would be well to amend this section. 1 do not think that the parties should go on and take action under this clause until their plans have been approved, and as there is no objection, I propose to insert, after the word ' aforesaid ' in the first line, the words ' after approval of the plans as provided in section 6 of this Act.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon James Sutherland).

speechtext: I would draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works to this clause. Most of the rights which the city would have to obtain would be those of easement for overflowing the lands, the right of erecting a dam and overflowing the lands. The principal damage would be the easement of the right of overflowing these lands. It seems to me they can do this without auy expropriation in the first instance. They would have the same right a railway would have. It is an extraordinary power to give to a person to erect a dam on a river.

In reply to the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary), I would say that the Bill had not been brought to my attention until after it had passed the committee. I would not like to refuse the city the legislation they are asking for, the object is a good one, and under certain restrictions it is desirable, perhaps, that the city of Winnipeg should have this power. But I think my hon. friend will agree with me that after the amendment we have put in for the approval of the plans, they can take action under this and under the Railway Act, and the city would be liable for all damages caused.
Under section 110 they have the power.

That is the power that is only given to a person to erect a dam on a navigable or other river. They can obtain the easement in the first place before they get the charter or the right to proceed. Tills gives them the power of erecting a dam and settling for the easements afterwards the same as the railway company may do. I think It is rather an extraordinary power to give to any person the right of overflowing a large section of country such as the hon. gentleman describes.

I would suggest that we might proceed with the Bill. Some material amendments have been proposed, and when the measure has passed through the committee stage it might stand for a third reading so that we might have an opportunity of further studying some of the suggestions which have been made to-day.

I think the amendment proposed by the hon. minister covers the case

in a fairly satisfactory manner. This is not a new matter. These powers hare been granted over and over again by this parliament. The question of damages has been thoroughly gone into. The dam is to be constructed within the corporate limits of the city of Winnipeg, and the area of the land which will possibly be damaged will not be more than 100 acres. All this has been provided for and there is no intention on the part of the city of Winnipeg to endeavour to exercise any extraordinary powers.
The city would be responsible for any damage done ?
Yes, the city makes itself thoroughly responsible for all damages.

I rather think the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) has not given the matter sufficient consideration. I have the statement of the engineers of the department here to the effect that instead of 100 acres being flooded it will be more like 10,000 or 20,000 acres. We all know that the banks of the Assiniboine at Head-wich, further up than Winnipeg are lower than they are at Winnipeg, and that as a result the country would be flooded. The hon. member for Provenclier (Mr. LaRiviere) knows that the Manitoba government, away back in 1881, constructed this very canal from Long lake to Assiniboine river, and that while it cost $10,000 or $15,000 to construct it, it cost nearly $50,000 to stop it up again because the water flooded the adjacent country. When I first went to Manitoba, the parish of Bale St. Paul was a populous parish, but in 1882, practically the whole population left and went to the North-west Territories, because of the flooding of the country ; in fact, in the town of Baie St. Paul, in the fall of 18S2, when the Canadian Pacific Railway was diverted from the route intended to Portage La Prairie which it was originally (intended to follow, X came down and I saw some of the houses which had been upset in that parish so deep had the water been. It is of some importance to the public that their rights should be safeguarded. WThen the hon. member for Winnipeg makes the statement that the construction of this dam may result in the overflowing of 100 acres of land he certainly is entirely in error. I have applied to the engineers of the department who understand the situation fairly well and they say that it will be impossible to construct a dam there without overflowing a large extent of territory. Under all the circumstances, I think the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) is quite right in suggesting that the Bill should stand until he has time to look into it.

It does not seem to be necessary to go into disasters that happened in other parts of the country in connection with this Bill. I have been in the city of Mr. PUTTEE.
Winnipeg during the last week looking into this question and examining the plans. I find that the plans are identical with those which were approved in 1889. The banks of the Assiniboine are as low immediately west of Winnipeg as anywhere. The overflow will extend for four miles west of Winnipeg to the point where the river strikes Sturgeon creek and not to Headingly. The river-bed at Headingly is 25 feet higher than it is at Winnipeg, and to say that* the land will be affected by the rise of the river level at that point is to say something which is not reasonable. As a matter of fact, It was stated in this House last week that these floods occurred last year right back as far as Portage La Prairie. Last year the water was higher than this dam when constructed will allow it to go. This dam will not stop the floodiug, but it will not increase it one bit. The water will only be raised as far back as Sturgeon creek four miles above the dam, and not up as far as Headingly where the banks are steep.
Have there been any protests against this Bill ?
The Board of Trade of Winnipeg did make a protest, but during the week they have been looking into the amendments that have been proposed and they have agreed that they are satisfactory.

As a matter of fact, the people there do not know anything about the Bill that is before the House. I scarcely knew anything about it until a few days ago. They have had no means of knowing.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 7.

I would ask the promoter of this Bill to show cause why this clause should not be struck out altogether. I think it would be very objectionable.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. I gave notice of motion to the effect that section 7 be struck out and I believe the promoter of the Bill agrees with me on that. I believe there should be a provision that wherever any work is done by the city of Winnipeg outside its own limits and within the confines of the limits of another municipality the local municipality should have something to say in the matter. It is a fact that these works might cover ground in one, two, three or four municipalities. There is the municipality of Assiniboia which is adjacent to the city of Winnipeg. They should be consulted if any work affecting their interests is done within their limits. The municipalities of St. Franqois-Xavier and Portage La Prairie are in the same position and therefore when my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) speaks with regard to those localities, he

speaks with regard to municipalities which he represents in this House ; namely the municipalities of Assiniboia and St. Fran-cois-Xavier. Of course that has no reference to this clause at all. I move that section 7 he struck out.

If that is the view taken well and good. However, if hon. gentlemen will look at the next clause they will see that this matter is thoroughly covered. The idea is that the putting up of this dam will practically make that river navigable and it has only been technically navigable for the last twenty years. Later, when necessary Work is done further along the river at Portage La Prairie perhaps by this government or the local government, the river for a considerable stretch will be navigable. At that time it would be right and proper that the lock should be put in. As the Minister of Public Works and the member for Provencher (Mr. LaRiviSre) think it is safer to have this clause striken out I agree but I point out that what they seek is already provided for in the Bill.

For the last fifteen years in the city of Winnipeg the question has been discussed of utilizing the power on the Assiniboine, and it has been a subject of a very great deal of investigation and study. It is a question to which very great importance is attached by the leading citizens of Winnipeg. and the House ought do what it can prudently do to enable the work to be carried out. There is however a great deal in what my hon. friend from Selkirk says in regard to the natural difficulties in the way, and I do not think that the House ought take any chances at all in regard to the rights of the property owners who live on the river banks above the city of Winnipeg. Whatever may be the importance of the wofk to the city of Winnipeg, it must be carried out in such a way as not to do injury to the rights of other people. In view of what happens in the Assiniboine river season after season it is difficult to think that the construction of a canal without a lock would be a safe proceeding. I am satisfied that the result of constructing a dam without a lock would sooner or later be disastrous, and in that respect I think that my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) is perfectly right. The Bill therefore should not give countenance to that intention, and when the time comes for the officers of the Department of Public Works to deal with this question, they will have to deal with it in a thorough and far reaching way, and they will have to have a complete examination made of the river for 100 miles or perhaps 150 miles, and a very careful study of the whole project, before approving of any plan. In the meantime it would be a great mistake for parliament j to give any indication that the works should
be built without any dam, and without any provision being made, not only for the purpose of navigation but in respect to the work itself.

There is an objection to transferring the power of eminent domain to the city of Winnipeg for the purpose of erecting a dam to create light and power. We transfer that power to companies for the purpose of constructing railways or canals, or telephone, or telegraph lines, but I have never known of it being transferred to a private company or to a city for the purpose of erecting a dam to generate light and power. I know the ground perfectly well, and it seems to me that this will be an enormous undertaking. A dam to be utilized for the purpose of power of any kind must flood the country for an immense distance up stream, and to allow any party to exercise that power without their plans being filed and the property acquired is a very serious matter.

It is merely a question of whether the purpose is of sufficient importance. I have known cases where power has been given for similar purposes. It is usual in some of the cities of the maritime provinces to give power to expropriate for the purpose of erecting water works, and the city of Halifax also received power to expropriate for the purpose of constructing a dry-dock. These are somewhat in the same line as the works proposed in this Bill except that in this case the city of Winnipeg is authorized to dispose of the surplus power for commercial purposes. As far as section 7 is concerned I do not think it makes the slightest difference, with regard to the power of the Governor in Council, whether it is in or out. If it is in, the Governor in Council may or may not order the lock, and if it is out, the Governor in Council may or may not order the lock. There is therefore no reason why it should not be struck out.

No doubt my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) is perfectly right as to the legal effect of section 7, but I am afraid that it might be an indication to the officers of the Department of Public Works that parliament had in mind the possibility of this being done without the construction of the lock. To that extent it seems to me the clause is objectionable and ought to come out. I do not think there is any serious objection to the city of Winnipeg, if it so desires, developing this i power and making use of it for any purpose it thinks fit. I remember that when the project was first mentioned the city authorities had the idea that they would lease the surplus power t'>
manufacturers, and that was the main purpose of the scheme at that time. And although I have not followed the discussions lately I feel satisfied that that idea is largely responsible for this Bill being

here. I can see no objection to their selling the surplus power in any manner they see fit.
I have no objection to their utilizing the power for any purpose whatever, but what I take exception to is granting to the city the right of expropriation for any such power as this.

I quite agree that every precaution should be taken to prevent the city from acting in an oppressive way or injuring in any way the private rights of anybody. Perhaps *when the sections have been further proceeded wtith, with the exception of this section 5, that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works may very well take that point into consideration.

I think a clause should be introduced stating more exactly what damages should be paid in case land was flooded. For some time past the city of Winnipeg has been trying to make an agreement with the Canadian Pacific Railway in respect to a subway, and in the Bill it was stated specifically what damages the Canadian Pacific Railway would have to pay. The Canadian Pacific Railway refused to enter into that agreement. It was stated that they must pay for the damages on Point Douglas Avenue as well as for five or six streets north and south of Point Douglas Avenue; so much so that the damages might have amounted to $1,000,000. If the city of Winnipeg was so careful in protecting its rights in that Bill why should they not grant the same protection to private individuals now ? The only means of crossing the Assiniboine river is by means of ferries, there are no bridges at all until you get to Portage La Prairie. There are ferries at St. James, and St. Charles, Headingly and St. Francois Xaxier, and if the river is made navigable these municipalities would be put to extra expense in operating these ferries. The cable would have to be lowered every time a boat came along, which would entail quite a little expense on the municipality. Outside of that the damage which should be assessed in favour of the private individual should be more fully stated in the Bill. He should not be put off with the bare value of his land on the edge of the river.
Motion of (Mr. LaRiviere) agreed to.
On section 10,

Here is the danger point in this Bill. While you have the city of Winnipeg to attack for damages, you are able to get justice, because it is a solvent corporation. But suppose that the city under this clause should assign the franchise and the works to a company which became insolvent, where would the private owner be ? The Bill does not make the city re-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: sponsible; it simply provides that the city may assign, and the party to whom it assigns shall be responsible. I think the owners of the land along the river should be better safe-guarded by this clause, if it is allowed to stand at all.

So far as I am able to judge, the hon. member is quite correct. It is questionable whether the power which we are granting to the city of Winnipeg would be granted to a private company. I think it would be only right to strike out this clause; and if at any future time the city should desire to transfer its rights to a company, it should come and ask for legislation for that purpose. It would be very mueli safer. I move that this clause be struck out.

Might I ask the hon. minister if the object he has in view could not be accomplished by amending this clause so as to require the city to obtain the consent of the Governor in Council before it assigns or transfers its rights ?
That was my first thought; but after hearing the discussion, I see that the interests involved are very large.
The city will have to assume all responsibility for whatever damage is sustained.
No, no.
As I understand, the city wants to construct these works and hand them over to a private company. It wants to control them, but to allow somebody else to operate them.
No, the city can assign the franchise.

I do not see how it would help the matter to require the city to obtain the consent of the Governor in Council. The city might hand over the franchise to people of straw. It is questionable, in my mind, whether such powers should be granted to the corporation at aff; because, by being allowed to transfer, the city gets' out of the responsibility. As to Orders in Council, they are not to protect rights, but to see that provisions made by parliament are properly carried out. An Order in Council would be no protection to the private owner against the objection to giving the city these extraordinary powers. If we gave them to the city, it would be on the consideration that it is a municipality and that it is responsible for all its acts; but I would even hesitate before giving such extensive powers to a city. We are, in fact, substituting the city for the Crown, giving it to some extent the right to control the navigation of this river. I think with the Minister of Public Works that we go quite far enough in giving the city power to construct these works, and if subsequently

it wants to transfer them to anybody else, it would be no hardship to it to come back for special legislation for that purpose.

I have two objections. I do not see why we should permit the city to transfer the water works anyway, because the city is the proper party to own and control water works. Secondly, 1 think we would be going a little too far to allow the transfer on its being submitted to the Governor in Council. I doubt very much the wisdom of permitting the Governor in Council to say that any franchise should he transferred. Some of the clauses I would not agree to if proposed for a private company; and if I would not for a private company, neither should I for the city if the city could transfer, to a private company; for so long as there is the power of transferring, it is the same as if we gave the franchise to a private company direct. I think this clause should be struck out, and all the other clauses referring to assignment amended so that we would give a charter to the city without the possibility of its being assigned to anybody else.

I would be sorry if it were possible to conceive of the city of Winnipeg obtaining this Act in its own name for the purpose of constructing certain works merely as a blind, in order to grant that power to a private corporation. I understood, from glancing at the Bill, that the [DOT]object of the city was to construct these works and have them operated by a private company, and that is the reason it asks for the power to assign. If this is .merely an attempt of the city to obtain for private Individuals legislation which they could not obtain for themselves, I have no objection to having this clause struck out; but I cannot conceive it possible that the city of Winnipeg would come and ask for legislation to benefit a few private individuals in the name of the city. I assume that if the city did assign its powers and franchises it would require those to whom it assigned to put up the necessary security before undertaking the work, and that if the Governor in Council were satisfied with the parties and the security, there would be no objection to allowing this clause to pass.
The danger to the property owners might arise after a great part of the work was done; and, after the city made the transfer, it would be relieved of responsibility.
They must give security.

No, they may, for the purpose of construction, alteration and everything else, transfer their rights and powers to any company upon such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between the city and such company. If we were dealing with a private corporation, we would hesitate a great deal before granting it any such rights, and we ought
to hesitate before granting the city this exceptional power and enabling it to get rid of all responsibility by transferring all its rights and obligations to a company. There might be question of very serious damages arising from the construction of the works authorized by this Bill for which the city would be responsible, and the question for us to consider is whether we shall allow the city to shift that responsibility upon somebody else.

The point which suggests itself to me is this :	Has
this House the authority to vest in the city of Winnipeg the power to interfere with provincial rights ? I should imagine that the provincial government would have something to say with regard to the carrying on of the works authorized by this measure.
I do not know what the opinion of the Department of Justice would be. but as these are navigable waters, we have no doubt the right to pass this legislation.
The canal is not navigable because it is solid land.
It would be after it was built.
Under the charter of the city of Winnipeg, I very much doubt if it has authority to build canals and navigate the Assiniboine river.

It might be necessary for the city to get legislation from the provincial legislature as well, with regard to some of these works, but so far as we are going we are acting within our jurisdiction. I move in amendment that this clause be struck out.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I ruled the other day that no amendment could be made to a Bill in Committee of the Whole, which was )of any importance, without giving a day's notice. To strike out a whole section is a very important amendment, and the rule to which I refer must apply.

Then I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, and I would ask you, Mr. Chairman, to take notice that at the next sitting of the committee I will move that this clause be struck out.

Was our action irregular in striking out clause 7 ?
Mr. LaRIVIERE. I gave notice of that.

I would ask the hon minister of Public Works to consider whether it would not serve the purpose just as well to put in a clause making this matter subject to the approval of the Governor in

Council. The city lias been asking for this power for years past, because tbis motive power is witbin the city limits, and tbe question of obtaining power is becoming a very serious one. We have no fuel except at a tremendous price, and tbe number of factories is growing. It seems to me that if we made tbis clause 10 subject to tbe approval of tbe Governor in Council, tliat would meet the difficulty witli regard to damages.
Motion agreed to, and progress reported.

And I watched it very closely, because the Bill is one calculated to interfere with existing rights, and it was my duty, associated with other gentlemen in connection with an existing charter, to protect those rights, and more especially so, in the absence of others, I was about the only one left to do it. This Bill is almost as broad in its scope as the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill, and it opens up a very large field. I have never taken up the time of the House discussing the Grand Trunk measure, or any other : but. as this opens such a wide scope. maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
What is the length of the proposed line ?
Hon. Mi*. COSTIGAN. Speaking roughly, I should think a couple of thousand miles. Two or three years ago a charter was applied for and obtained to construct a road from some point opposite the city of Quebec down through the province of Quebec and into the province of New Brunswick, so as to connect with the railways existing at that time. That charter was obtained as the result of a consultation between several Quebec representatives and myself in the province of New Brunswick. We had felt a great desire to have wliat we contended for in the early days, the old Intercolonial line extended, and, though we failed to secure the construction of that road by the route which we thought the most economical and the best, we did obtain the construction of the line built from Fredericton up as far as Edmunston at a cost, not to this country but to our province, of tbe most valuable wild farming lands in the Dominion of Canada-bush lands. We reached Edmundston. We made further efforts to get the line built thirty-five miles farther, to a point near the mouth of the St. Francis. Twelve or fifteen years ago. during the time when Mr. Merrier was in power in Quebec, a charter was granted to construct the Quebec portion, not in connection witli ours, but as a colonization road. It was to develop the lands in six counties in the province of Quebec, on the south shore of the St. Lawrence. The province of Quebec granted a bonus of 12,000 acres of land per mile in afd of the road. Land at that time was not considered as valuable as it is at present; and, having no other subsidy, the company failed to build that colonization road in the province of Quebec. Having pushed that railway thirty-five miles up beyond Edmundston towards the western country, towards Quebec, I approached the late Mr. Deschenes, who was a member of this House, and who was working up the enterprise of having this road built through Quebec. 1 told him that if he would join us in New Brunswick and make it an interprovincial railway, our chances would be better, and I would do anything to work with him if he would agree to connect at Connors' station or at the present terminus of the Temiscouata branch of the line. This was arranged, and we obtained the charter. Everything went on satisfactorily. The Dominion government gave a subsidy to about half the road, that is 135 miles to the point of connection at Connors' station.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Does this go by the St. Francis river ?

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Yes. The province of New Brunswick granted its usual subsidy for the portion in that province to encourage the construction of this through line : and the Dominion parliament granted a subsidy for half the whole line. The Que-

bee legislature did not grant the aid that was expected by the Quebec friends. Last year a contract was entered into with the Dominion government to construct the first section on the lower end. Work was commenced and proceeded with. This session my attention was called to the fact that amongst other charters one was applied for to construct a railway from the city of Quebec up to the Quebec bridge, across the bridge and thence to Moncton, thence to some point in Nova Scotia, and so through the province of Nova Scotia to some harbour on the eastern coast of Nova Scotia.
I do not think I am over suspicious ; but, looking around. I wondered at the application being made for a charter which must necessarily blanket the charter of the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway Company ; and, more than that, was evidently intended to blanket or cover the charter already granted to another company two years ago,
I believe, to build from the city of Quebec up to the Quebec bridge and control its approaches. Now, 1 wondered why this application should be made to construct the railway from the city of Quebec up to that bridge, which must cover this existing charter. I was more surprised at that than at the attempt to cover the charter claimed by the Quebec and New Brunswick charter. One of the reasons that I asked that the Bill should go back is this-and this is the effect of the amendment of which I gave notice, but which I cannot discuss now- that the line should be defined to some extent. at least the proposed location of the road through the province of Quebec. Now. some of the hon. gentlemen who are behind this Bill say that they do not intend to touch or interfere with the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway. That is all very well. But the charter does not say that-the charter leaves them full power to construct over every mile in Quebec and New Brunswick of the Quebec and New Brunswick charter. I do not think that that is right. I did propose to some of these gentlemen, when they told me they did not want to lmild over the line of the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway, but to take a short cut through Maine : Amend your Bill ; be frank, and say you are going to build from Quebec to a point on the boundary, and name the point. From that you can secure your right through the state of Maine. Let us know where you are going to. But that has not been done. The Bill was passed in committee and comes from committee in this shape, giving them the power, if they wish to exercise it, to build over every mile of road chartered and under contract with this government. I do not think that is a fair proposition at all. It has been said that I raised no objections on behalf of the company that I am speaking for. when the Grand Trunk Bill was in committee. It is true I did not make any protest on that ground, because
I understood that all the people of the eastern provinces were a unit, or ought to be a unit, and I am sure they are, on any question affecting a transcontinental line, when they are seeking an outlet at some Canadian port in the east. I felt there was no doubt about that. If I raised any question for my part as to how they would reach that eastern port in Canadian territory it might be said that I was inconsistent, that while I was pressing this corporation to extend their line in Quebec eastward down to the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, I was throwing obstacles in the way of their doing so. I felt all the time, though interested as president and one-of the directors of the road, that if the company were to build a transcontinental line down to the sea-board, and to build it through Canadian territory, there was no other ground for it to take but over that line.
I really thought at the same time that we should not stand there in the position of stand and deliver, and say :	You cannot
go over there without you pay so much. If the country wanted a through-line we were entitled to take that position, and I believe they will take it yet, whoever constructs the road. But because I was willing to do that, and the company I represent, I daresay, was willing to do that, as this was the only proposition that came before the House as a transcontinental line, that is no reason why our company should sit down and allow a Bill like this to pass this House, taking away rights granted by this parliament and recognized by the government, from a company that is now under contract with the government for the construction of this very road. I do not think it is consistent at all, I do not think that hon. gentlemen ought to press this any further. I simply ask :	Do the company
wish to ignore the legislation of this parliament and deprive the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway of their charter? If they do, then I must say that I will do my best to oppose it. Are they sincere in stating that they do not want to interfere with that road at all, but that they want to go across the state of Maine ? Very well, if they do, let them amend their Bill, or ask that it be sent back to the committee where that amendment may be made. Here is the first clause of the Bill :
' The company may lay out, construct and operate a railway of the gauge of four feet and eight and a half inches, from a point in the city of Quebec to the Quebec bridge on the north shore of the river St. Lawrence, and may enter into an agreement with the Quebec Bridge Company for operating the new line of railway over the bridge of the said Quebec Bridge Company, and thence by the most convenient route from the south shore approach of said bridge to a point at or near Moncton.
That is their starting point. We start at Chaudiere Junction near Quebec, and we go in the most convenient direction-not to ' Moncton, because our charter never content-

plated such a line at that time. But so far as it goes it covers the only ground possible in Canadian territory for a transcontinental line to follow. I understand that some slight change has been made in the Bill in committee in regard to one part of the line when it reaches Moncton. I think the Minister of Railways very properly considered that that paralleled the Intercolonial too closely.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Beyond Moncton ?

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Near Moncton. It was considered to parallel the Intercolonial, and was therefore amended. I would like also to see the Bill amended in such a waJ? that the rights acquired by Canadian subjects from this parliament, rights which they are legitimately and lawfully enjoying, are not interfered with. I rise to oppose and to protest against this House being iOsk-eil to ignore that company by granting a charter which, in the very wording of it, takes away rights that have already been acquired, which would ignore the company entirely. I presume, Mr. Speaker, that on that motion being carried for you to leave S'?ail'>
we would go into committee on the Bill. Now I do not like to take the position of standing here and wearying the House. I think I have said enough'to show that I have pretty good reasons for making objection to the progress of this Bill in its present shape. If you leave the Chair and tile House goes into committee, I will have other and more convenient opportunities of discussing it, because I would rather speak often than a long time at once.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman how much road his company has completed, how much road has been completed by the New Brunswick and Quebec Railway Company ?

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Without giving full details, I will give the information that has been given to the Committee of Railways and Canals with respect to this Bill. The company have done all that is necessary to hold their rights under the charter, and they have complied with the law in every respect so far as I know, both in subscribing their stock and in conducting their business, in taking a contract from the government to build a portion of the road, in commenc-, ing the work within the time stipulated, in' buying and paying for the right of way, and in many other ways. But I do not wish to give any more details. If the company has forfeited its charter, then let that be said.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: How much of it have you built on the River St. Francis, for Instance ?

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: We have only started. I do not suppose there has been [DOT]over $20,000 expended on it.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: But is not a part of that line built ?

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: No, we only commenced last year. We could not get the rails. When I made the inquiries myself I found we could not get first class Canadian rails, they told us the best they could do was to give us English rails, first class rails delivered at Quebec for $45 a ton, and we would have to pay for carrying them across to L6vis and the freight from there down; so we did not buy the rails. But that question is entirely aside from the question asked me. It is true the gentleman who asked me the question may say that behind him are men who will do a great deal more. I think perhaps they would. But we have done all that the law required us to do. If not, let them show that the company is in default and let them wipe out the charter. But the charter is not wiped out, the charter is in existence and legally in force, and their contract is in existence.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Was not this matter discussed before committee 5

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The Bill was never discussed in committee. The promoter of the Bill told me he would not bring it in my absence. I was away, and he kept his word. The next day there was a meeting of the committee,-and the Bill was called. I was in the city, but not in the committee, and when I came to the House, and went upstairs, I found that another gentleman, not knowing the discussion that had taken place between us. had called the Bill, in good faith, I daresay. The Bill went through, but there was no discussion, that is, there was no chance so far as I was concerned as representing the other company, and no chance for me to offer any opposition, or to ask for any amendment in that committee. I think the Bill ought to go back to the committee to be amended.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I am sorry that I cannot oblige the hon. member for Victoria, N.B. (Hon. Mr. Costigan). I think if ever a man had a weak case when asking for a Bill to be sent back to the committee, the hon. member has shown a weak case to-day. I am not going to occupy the time of the House at present, and I regret that the hon. gentleman has seen fit to throw out the threat that he is going to weary the House by talking upon this question, when it goes into committee and so on. The facts of the matter are that the Bill providing for the construction of the Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia Railway is a Bill to allow of a construction of a railway to connect with the Great Northern Railway. That railway is at present controlled by Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann, and this Bill authorizes them to connect that railway with a maritime province port. It is a well known fact that the Canadian Northern Railway, or

597S
the Mackenzie & Mann system of railways, control the Canadian Northern Railway through the province of Quebec which gives them a summer port. They desire to secure a winter port, and for that purpose they are,
I think, entitled to get this charter which is before the House at the present time. Now, the hon. member for Victoria is a director of the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway Company. I am not going to discuss the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway Company. If it becomes necessary to discuss the progress of that company, I think I might be able to show that the progress lias not been such as will commend the enterprise to this House, but I do not think it worth while to discuss that, because of the position it occupies at the present time. The Bill which is now before the House was before the Railway Committee for a considerable length of time. I knew that there were some gentlemen interested in it and I spoke to them and asked them when it would be convenient for us to discuss the Bill in the Railway Committee. It never was convenient until last Thursday, when the hon. member for Victoria came to me and said that he desired to attend a picnic on Thursday, and asked me if I would agree to allow the Bill to go over. While it had been hanging for a long time, I allowed the Bill to go over, although the hon. gentleman did not go to the picnic, but happened to be in the committee. The Bill was brought up on Friday last. I was there myself. The Bill was discussed, it was amended at the suggestion of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair), it went through without a dissenting vote, and now we are asked, when it comes up here by the unanimous consent of the Railway Committee, amended and endorsed by the Minister of Railways and Canals, which amendments were accepted by me as the promoter of the Bill, to consent to send this Bill back to the committee simply because the hon. member for Victoria did not happen to be in the committee, and because the hon. gentleman happens to be a director of another company which has a charter for a small part of the country over which this charter authorizes the construction of a line. I do not think he has made out a case that will commend itself to this House.
Mi-. CLARKE. How far would your road parallel his ?

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not know that it will parallel it at all. I think there is room enough for all ; but that aside, the application for this charter was made before the application for the Grand Trunk Railway charter. Now, we have granted the charter to the Grand Trunk Railway. I am willing that another road that is going to be a transcontinental road shall also get down there. They simply come and ask for the passage of this Bill. The argument of the hon. member for Victoria (Hon. Mr. Costigan) is no good when you consider that this House has passed the Grand Trunk Railway Bill. Now the Grand Trunk Railway Bill, will kill him, and he cannot be killed any worse by a second Bill. The fight, if there is to be a fight, will be between the Grand Trunk Railway and this company. He is dead already if there is anything in liis contention, because the Grand Trunk Railway Bill is passed, authorizing it to construct to Moncton, an all-Canadian route through Canadian territory.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: It has not passed yet.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: It has passed through the committee and it is going to pass through this House ; so that, there is nothing gained and there is nothing that the hon. gentleman has to fear. As the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) said in the committee, before a road is in operation, if two or more parties come and ask for a charter, give it to them. After a road is built, equipped and in operation, there are rights that should be respected. But I think, now that the Grand Trunk Railway Bill has passed the committee. Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann have the right to the Bill which they desire to enable them to connect with their own road and to connect with the lower provinces. Therefore, I cannot see any ground for sending the Bill back.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Have the gentlemen of whom the hon. member for Victoria (Hon. Mr. Costigan) speaks lost any time in going on with their work since they got their charter ?

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Much time.
Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the Bill.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not want to get into any personal discussion with any of my hon. friends in this House, but I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Logan) in whose name the Bill stands was a little in error when he stated the conditions upon which the Bill stood over. He said that I had asked him after his arrangements were made and when his friends had found it convenient to meet and take up the Bill on a certain day, to have the Bill held over because I wanted to go to a picnic. No, I did not ask that at all. We discussed the Bill, and it is true I stated I was going to a picnic, and I did go to a picnic. Notwithstanding the fact that the hon. gentleman said I was present in the committee, I did go to the picnic.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: And I had a very pleasant time.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: That was on Thursday ?

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: It was on Dominion day. On Thursday the committee met again.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The committee did not meet on Dominion day.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Then there were two picnics.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The other fellows had the picnic next day.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Yes, the picnic was here the next day. I was absent from that unfortunately. I feel myself a little embarrassed in speaking as I do and in opposing a charter behind which stand men for whom I have the greatest respect and in whose ability to build a railway I have the greatest confidence. If that firm had come forward to this parliament and proposed to build an all-Canadian transcontinental line I would have held up both hands for it in preference to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. The hon. gentleman who promotes this Bill says that he does not want to go into a discussion of the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway Company or their affairs. Well, I am glad of that, but I hope he does not want to create the impression that there is anything in the transactions of that company which the company are afraid to discuss openly in parliament. The company have been properly organized, as I have said before, and I cannot see the necessity of this Bill. It is true there is a small portion of the line of the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway Company in my own constituency, and so far as the rights of my constituents are concerned, I feel it is my duty as well as my right to speak for and advocate their interests and rights. It passes through six counties in Quebec, and I know that every one of these six counties wants that road constructed and has been waiting for it for years. The people in these counties have been promised the road and they want to see it constructed. The question has been asked of the promoter of this Bill, how far the company behind this charter would be likely to parallel the existing line of the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway, and now an hon. gentleman says: Well, I do not know but I think there is room for several railways there. That might be, if you could build railways irrespective of the formation of the country. But there is notably but one single available line open for a railway there, and that is to follow the St. Francis valley, or if you go to the state of Maine you can get through .the St. John valley, but you would have to pass through American territory. By following the St. Francis valley you can keep in Canadian territory and get good grades. That is the reason why the Quebec and New Brunswick Company took that particular route. There is just one point, and it is very pronounced on some of the maps, that juts in there
and our company could have shortened its line twelve or fourteen miles by cutting across that nose of land, but we would have to go through American territory, and we would not have got as good grades. Why is it that the gentlemen in charge of this Bill are not a little more definite in their location of the railway. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Logan) defines the line from the city of Quebec right up the north shore of the St. Lawrence. There is only one place there where you could go and get to the bridge and cross the bridge to the approach on the south side. But when they get to the south side they propose to reach a point at or near Moncton without one syllable in the Bill to indicate by which route they are going to get there. When the promoter of the Bill defines his line so plainly from the city of Quebec to Chaudiere Junction, why is it that he does not define the route from Chaudiere to Moncton. Will it come between the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway and parallel the Intercolonial along the borders of the St. Lawrence? If it does it will have to follow that route all the way, because we all know that the Temiscouata Railway was built across that country from River du Loup to the valley of St. John and the grades on that road are such as to make it almost impossible to carry on a business traffic on that road. Successful railway operation to-day has resolved itself into a question of good road-bed and light grades, and you cannot handle traffic, nor can you pretend to successfully give an outlet to products of the west unless you have such a road as will handle the greatest amount of traffic with the least expenditure of power. Some persons have said that we ought not be uneasy because they do not intend to touch our road at all. Well, they are going from Chaudi&re to Moncton, and if they <2o not go by the valley of the St. Lawrence or by the valley of the St. Francis or through the air, they will have to go through the state of Maine. I admit that it is shorter for them to go through the state of Maine, but if they intend to do that why don't they say so ? I do not ask that the Bill should specify what particular parts of Maine they should go through, because we have no right to say anything about that, but let them indicate what route they will take after they get to Chaudiere Junction. Why should this parliament allow them to take a route that will practically destroy an existing charter which is now in process of being worked out. If it is the contention of these gentlemen that the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway have not made more rapid progress, I can tell them that we have reasonably complied with the requirements of our Act and this very session parliament has passed a Bill extending the time for the extension of our charter, putting us in a position to go on with the work. It is true

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: that we liaye been delayed and one of the causes of delay was that financial arrangements could not be made until the government of Quebec had aided the portion of the line going through that province, there being about 110 miles, out of a total of 135 in the province of Quebec.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: How would the proposed Grand Trunk Pacific Railway arrangement affect you financially ?

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not know what form the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme will take, nor do I know what it will be when it gets to this parliament.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Nobody else seems to know much about it.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I presume that if a transcontinental line is to be built it will be carried through to some Canadian port on the Atlantic. I would not complain if the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway would absorb the Quebec and New Brunswick. As one man I will say that I have no desire to block a great enterprise like that, but because I am willing to go that far, [DOT]does it mean that I am going to give the same concession to another company. It is true the promoters of this Bill say that it is part of a transcontinental line.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: There are three miles of it partly finished.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I suppose there is a good deal of grading done ?

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The grading is partly done, the right of way bought and paid for, and the plans and surveys over the . first section made and approved of by the Governor tin Council.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: You are not default in your charter ?

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: No, and we have been able to show that or parliament would not have extended the time.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: What suggestion have you got to make with regard to the other charter ?

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I suggest that they should define their line from Ohaudiere Junction to Moncton more distinctly. Do they want to go over the road we propose to build or do they want to go to the left of it. All I ask them to say is that they will agree to a clause stating that it shall not be prejudicial to our charter.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: When was your charter first obtained ?

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Part of the Mackenzie & Mann scheme.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I have no desire to throw any obstacle in their way, but I have naturally a very strong desire to see that there should be some respect paid to what little rights we have there. I am well aware that I may have to submit to the forces that are behind this Bill and that I may have nothing for my trouble but a little talk, but whether that be so or not, I intend to talk very plainly about it. I say that if this charter passes through it will cause disappointment to a great many people in the province of Quebec and in the province of New Brunswick as well. It will cause more than disappointment. I think I would have the right to complain that there is a want of good faith somewhere. The first subsidy was granted by the federal parliament to the Quebec and New Brunswick road for three miles of that road extending from Connors' Station to the mouth of the St. Francis before the charter was obtained. Then when the charter was obtained, the Dominion government subsidized sixty miles of the whole road, making sixty-three miles of a Dominion subsidy, and forty-five miles of that subsidy was put on the Quebec end and fifteen miles upon the New Brunswick end so as to give assurance to the people of both the provinces interested that the road would not be diverted to any other place.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: How many miles of it is built ?

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
In 1900 or 1901. As far as the charter is concerned, if any one wishes to argue that the company has not made great progress I plead guilty to that. I do not want to make any dishonest claim or profession. We made no great progress for the reason I have stated. The railway runs through six counties in the province of Quebec and only through one county in the province of New Brunswick, and over 100 miles out of the 130 is situated in the province of Quebec. We were waiting until the government of the province of Quebec could grant aid for that portion of the line running through that province. But we made the commencement on the New Brunswick end, where we had a subsidy. We made a contract, we have not forfeited our contract, we bought the right of way and paid for it, we made our survey, and we came to this parliament this session, I acting for the company, and asked for an' extension of time. The Bill passed this House and the Senate, and we got the extension of time. I do not think it is a strong argument to criticise the legal standing of the company. It is a fair argument to say that we have not made very rapid progress. I admit that. It is no argument to say that the gentlemen who are seeking this charter are men who would push this road vigorously. I believe that too. But if they are going to build through Maine, I have not the same interest in the road, nor have I the same objection to it. This is not a matter I am now prepared to discuss ; but I think I am entitled to have

some explanation as to tbe location of the road.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: It is impossible definitely to say that. But this company is composed of some of the best men in Canada. The man who represents it in Nova Scotia, Mr. Graham Fraser, is a man whose name is a household word. The idea is to go through Canadian territory, if such can be done ; but they simply ask for the chance of building and operating by the most convenient route. They cannot say anything more. They cannot name the places through which they would build because the places they might name here might not furnish the best route. I think the hon. gentleman's fears will be found to be groundless. For myself I want to see the railroad built through Canadian territory. I do not know the best route, but if it is impossible to build it through Canadian territory, and if the hon. gentleman's line is to be built as well as the Grand Trunk, perhaps they may get a charter for a line through Maine. But in the meantime, as the Grand Trunk is to be built to Moncton, I think we should not prevent these people getting a charter to do the same thing. If any injury is done to the hon. gentleman's scheme, it has been done already by the Grand Trunk.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The Grand Trunk Bill is not passed yet.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Well, it is as good as passed. They are going to get their Bill. We were in the field first. Mackenzie and Mann -want this system in order to connect with the lower provinces and to reach Moncton by the most convenient route. I think my hon. friend will find that his interest will not be at all prejudiced, and that nothing will be done to interfere with his route. I am sure that Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann are broad minded enough not to hurt his road. But I must come back to the other argument, because it strikes me as a complete answer, that already there is a Bill before this House, which is sure to go through the House, which puts him in that position already.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I do not want to weary the House, or to obstruct, or to keep other Bills behind ; but I do say that there is a regular way of proceeding. I obtained information as to the steps I could take, and, after getting advice, I had a notice prepared, finding that I must give notice of an amendment to this Bill, and it is in the hands of the clerk. It will not appear before to-morrow, so that I shall have no chance of moving it till then. Under these circumstances, I think it is a little hard to forces this Bill through. The hon gentlemen have a strong combination behind them, but they ought not to use their strength to force this Bill through, when I say that it is not Hon. Mr. COSTIGAN.
a fair thing to do. I am assured that tins charter will not hurt us-that its promoters only desire to take the most convenient route. Well, a very convenient thing for a new company to do is to work on the experience of forty years, and to take the only convenient route recognized in that country. When the Intercolonial Railway was undertaken, a line was surveyed through the St. Francis river country, and it was the line approved of.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: What is the hon. gentleman's amendment ?

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The amendment is that the Bill shall go back to the committee, and define the proposed route approximately through the province of Quebec, if no further.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: That is not done in the Grand Trunk Bill, and, if my memory serves me rightly, in the hon. gentleman's own Bill the definite points one after another are not named.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not think there is anything in the hon. gentleman's contention that we should define the exact points where this road shall run. We have passed many Bills through this House in which the paints are not defined. Unexpected difficulties may arise, and we must give some latitude to the people who are putting large sums of money into these enterprises. The hon. member for Victoria, N.B., is the last man whose interests we desire to prejudice. He said we have a good deal of strength behind us, and I think we have a good deal of strength In this House. As the promoter of the Bill, I will agree that the location of the line be subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. I do rot think I could do anything fairer than that.

maintopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Victoria, N.B. (Hon. Mr. Costigan) has to my knowledge been promoting this railway for a number of years. It runs through his own county, and through the St. Francis river country to Ghaudiere Junction, and it has what I think the only feasible connection, so far as gradients are concerned, between New Brunswick and the Chaudiere bridge. He says there was a load built via Temiscouata, but its gradients were such that it could not be used for freight purposes at all. House went into committee on Bill (No. 157) to incorporate the Brandon, Saskatchewan and Hudson's Bay Railway Company.- Mr. Stewart.
On section 10,

maintopic: BRANDON, SASKATCHEWAN AND HUDSON'S BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Before section 10 is adopted, I have an amendment to propose. When this Bill was before the Railway Committee, there seemed to be some feeling on the part of the members of that committee that possibly there was little or no intention on the part of the promoters to construct this railway. I believe that a great many Bills are being introduced In this House to charter railway companies where the real intention of the promoters is unknown, no attempt being made to show that the provisional directors have the ability to build the road or have any real intention of proceeding with it. It is felt, I know, by other members of the committee besides myself that many of these Bills are simply put upon the statute book to give the provisional directors an opportunity of dealing with some company of real railway builders.
I realize that we are chartering far too many railways in that fashion, and I think some restriction should be put upon the power of these concerns to alienate their charters or holding up some railway company that wishes to construct a line of railway over the same route. If 188
the intention of the company is a genuine one, if they intend to construct the road and put it in operation, the amendment I now propose will in no way interfere with them. But if the charter is not intended to be acted upon by these promoters, if it is simply to be held until some other charter is asked for to build over the same territory and then to hold up the company asking for it, the amendment will have the effect of preventing the incorporators under this charter from interfering with or unduly harassing any company that may want to build the road. Section 10 reads as follows :-
The company may enter into an agreement with the Canadian Northern Railway Company or the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, for conveying or leasing to such company the railway of the company, in whole or in part, or any rights or powers acquired under this Act.
1 contend that this company should not be empowered to enter into any agreement to convey its charter or any of the rights that are given under this Bill until they have practically completed their road. If they have a bona tide intention of building the road, the amendment I propose will not hinder them, but it will prevent their holding up another railway company which might want to construct the road. Therefore. I move that after the word ' may,' in the first line of section 10, the following words be inserted : ' After the said railway has been constructed and put in operation, but not before.' The clause will then read :
' The company may, after such railway has been constructed and put in operation, but not before, enter into an agreement with the Canadian Northern Railway Company, the Canadian Pacific Railway,' and so on.

maintopic: BRANDON, SASKATCHEWAN AND HUDSON'S BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I am not interested in this Bill in any way, but I was in the Railway Committee when the same objection and the same proposition were made by the hon. member for Halton. Does it not strike the hon. gentleman that it is rather late in the day to propose an amendment of that kind ? We have up to the present, during this session and during preceding sessions, passed through railway Bills containing exactly the same clause. Why should we single out this particular scheme and apply this restriction to it ? While I entirely agree in the suggestion of the hon. member, because I do not believe in what is known as charter mongering, I do not see why we should impose a restriction in this Bill, at this stage of the session, which you have not imposed in any others of a similar nature. If we intend to apply the principle advocated by the hon. member, let us start at the beginning of a session with the first Bill before the Railway Committee, and then we will not be accused of unfairness and discrimination.

speechtext:
I do not consider that this amendment will in any way interfere



with the operations of the promoters if they really intend constructing this road.

speechtext: Does it not discriminate against them ?

maintopic: BRANDON, SASKATCHEWAN AND HUDSON'S BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman asks why this road should be singled out ?
I would simply reply that the evil has been a growing one, and we must begin some time to put a stop to it. Why should we not begin with this Bill ? I may relieve the hon. gentleman's mind if I tell him that to the end of this session I shall be very careful to propose the same amendment to every railway charter that comes before this House, when I have any suspicion that the promoters are simply getting the charter for the purpose of selling it. I am sorry the lion. Minister of Railways is not in his place, but I may say that he took a strong view in the Railway Committee on this question, and stated that next session of parliament he would deal with it, so that the only question is whether we should begin now or wait until another session. My impression is that now is the time to stop the evil, instead of waiting for another session, and possibly passing a dozen or two of charters before this session closes.
X hope, therefore, that the committee will accept this amendment, more especially as it will not prevent the construction of this road if the promoters are in earnest.

maintopic: BRANDON, SASKATCHEWAN AND HUDSON'S BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The amendment proposed is, in my judgment, very useful and important. If it affected no other object, it would probably save some weeks of the time of parliament every session. Hundreds of Acts are on the statute-books granting charters which were never obtained with the slightest idea on the part of the promoters of constructing the railways in ques-. tion. The promoters in each case simply spent a couple of hundred dollars to get through a charter in the hope of being able to sell it at a profit to somebody else, and the amendment suggested would put an end to that practice. Why incorporate companies and authorize them to sell railways which they have no intention of constructing ? If these various promoters had built their railways, there might be some reason for enabling them to sell or lease their property, but they simply get a charter and the power to sell it and put that charter on the market for sale. There is not an bon. member in this House who believes that in one charter out of ten granted here for the building of railways the promoters are competent to go on with the work. Their sole object is, not to build, to sell out their charter to some existing company at a profit, and thus pass on to some other company the very work wiiich we authorize them to construct. I think it is about time to put a stop to that sort of thing. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Gallilier) says we should not begin this session but wait until next session. But at the beginning of next ses-Mr. HENDERSON.
sion we will have the same objection raised again. There are scores of people paying out money to get Bills printed and drafted, and going to all sorts of expense, in the expectation of getting charters, with this clause inserted, giving them the right to sell ; and if we were to decide now that we would not give this right, we would save these people considerable expense and trouble. The best thing we can do is to take all the Bills coming before us this session and strike out this clause, and thus give full notice to all further applicants for railway charters what they may expect.

speechtext:
It seems strange that the voice of the hon. gentleman was never raised before against this prevailing iniquity. It has been said that the hon. Minister of Railways has given notice that next session he would deal with this matter. Well, that will go abroad. That is all I ask, I ask that this Bill be treated exactly the same as other Bills this session. If we have started in on a particular line and have followed it through during the present session so far, let us carry it out and be fair to all parties.
