Seeing the Minister of Customs in his seat, I desire to bring to his notice a subject of vital importance to the fishing and shipping interests of the maritime provinces.
The case I desire to present to the minister's notice is this ; The seizure of the schooner ' Markland.' The schooner ' Mark-land,' Captain Begin, Master, of 99 tons, belonging to the port of Mahone Bay, N.S., was returning some few weeks ago from the fishing grounds off Cape Breton, in Nova Scotia waters, her destination being the port to which she belonged-Mahone Bay-to discharge a small catch of fish, and owing to heavy weather, and a dense fog prevailing when off Halifax harbour, she put into that pore as a place of refuge, anchoring Jnside of Georges Island, having reached that port about 11 o'clock in the morning of the 15tl) of June, 1903, and the next morning at 5 o'clock-the 16th of June-weighed anchor and proceeded on her voyage. On the afternoon of the 15th, and whilst the vessel was at anchor, a boat drew up beside the vessel, and one of the boats' crew asked the deck hand, who chanced to be on the deck of the vessel at the time, where the vessel was from, and whither bound, which was answered, that they were from the fishing grounds off Cape Breton, and bound to Mahone Bay. Had this official asked for the captain of the 'Markland' and advised him of the requirements of the port and the necessity of his reporting inward, the captain would have complied with his request, which I contend the official should have done, and thereby avoided serious loss, and inconvenience, as well as annoyance to owners and fishermen. But instead of which, he-the Tide Waiter, or official, reported the vessel to flie officer of customs at Halifax, who acting on the information, advised the customs officer at Mahone Bay to seize the vessel for an offence of the Customs Act, requiring a bond, and deposit of $400-the maximum penalty-awaiting the decision of yourself, the minister here at Ottawa.

The master of the schooner informed me that he had great difficulty in obtaining the .$400-during which time the vessel was detained at a serious loss to owners and crew.
The master further stated that this was his first voyage as master, and that he was impressed with an idea that had he been in port 24 hours, he would have been required to report, but even on this he had a doubt, as tlfe vessel was engaged in fishing. As a fisherman merely entering the port for a place of refuge, and awaiting a chance to proceed on her voyage, not intending to land, or take anything on board and with no intent of wrong doing is a hardship which you yourself, Sir, I feel will realize, and which is recognized, I can assure you by all fishermen, and those engaged in shipping. as indeed cruel. And in view of the facts, I consider the owners and master should be released from the payment of any penalty, as they suffered sufficiently already from the action of the sub-official, in not- when he'was at the side of the vessel at Halifax asking for the captain, and informing him of what the port required-unless the object of the sub-official in not advising the master, was greed, plunder or ill-gotten gain, to supply his own pocket, in which case I contend lie should be severely reprimanded.
1 feel it my duty, Sir, to bring this matter to your notice considering it a great hardship that our vessel fishermen should be compelled to report at every port along the Nova Scotia shore they enter for refuge, or a supply of bait, when they have nothing to land, or take from the port. In fact I do not consider it was ever Intended that fishermen should be placed under such rigid ruling, as they would find themselves in such cases at a serious sacrifice to carry such ruling out, so much so that they would have to abandon the industry of fishing entirely.
With the manipulation of interests in the markets of the West Indies where the fish are principally disposed of, competitionbeing so keen, we can barely have a margin of profit at all, but if those engaged in deep-sea fishing are to be told, and required when their vessels enter a port for refuge or for bait that they must report to the Customs every time, I mean vessels engaged in the fisheries, and their vessels detained till the Customs official puts in an appearance in his office at ten o'clock in the morning, it would be extremely hard, and ns the representative of the largest fishing constituency in the Dominion, I strongly protest against such ruling, and ask that the Customs official of the port of Halifax, and every other port along the sea-girt shore, be advised that fishing vessels, actually engaged in fishing, shall when entering a port for shelter from a storm, or seeking bait, be relieved of reporting to the Customs, unless they are in port over twenty-four hours.
1 must ask the Minister of Customs to realize the serious inconvenience such ruling as I have referred to, such as was dealt out to the schooner ' Markland ' would be to the deep-sea fishermen, and the sacrifice to the fishing industry in general, in being so hampered by this unnecessary requirement, and I here ask the minister to have in future all fishing vessels actually engaged in fishing, relieved of such a requirement so unnecessary and unreasonable.

I may say to the hon. gentleman that had I known he wrould bring this matter to the attemion of the House this afternoon T would have refreshed my memory as to the particulars. However, I shall take care that the department will have its attention called to the remarks and suggestions of the hon. gentleman, and if it can be found with perfect safety that the line of action he suggests may be adopted, of course v*e would be prepared to adopt it. There is no desire to harass any one in that way, but, in order to prevent illicit traffic we have found it necessary to be a little more strict in reference 1o these matters than perhaps was hitherto the case. I will bring the suggestions of the hon. gentleman to the attention of the officers of the department.
lion. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.). I would like to say to the hon. member for Lunen-iierg (Mr. Kaulbach) that there will be no necessity for a vessel being detained until ten o'clock as she can enter at the customs house at nine o'clock in the morning. There is a steam boat in connection with the customs house that boards all the vessels that come into the port, and when the other side of the story will be known from the report made by- the officer himself, it will be found that he just warned the man he saw on deck that the vessel must report to the customs house. If you are going to widen this gap, and allow vessels to go into port and leave again without reporting within twenty-four hours, you do not know' the'mischief you are going to create. A part of my complaint the hon. member for Victoria, I do not think understands. My complaint is that this official who spoke the vessel lying at anchor in Halifax harbour, spoke to a deck-hand, whereas he should have asked for the master of the vessel, and should have informed him w'hat the requirements of the port yvere. My hon. friend from Victoria does not seem to realize this fact.

I realize this fact, that the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach) has the report from his captain, but where is the report which the Minister of Customs has from the collector at Halifax ? Because there are always two sides to a story of this kind.

It would seem that in this case the hon. Minister of Customs has not been informed of the circumstances, and therefore it is impossible to form any opinion as to whether a hardship has been improperly or unintentionally inflicted on the owners of the vessel or on the captain. But I would imagine, in view of the enormous number of fishermen employed about our coasts, and the absolute necessity there, is occasionally of their running into a port and out again, and the great importance of their not being delayed during the fishing season, that the" rule requiring them to report at the customs house should be waived if it can be done. However, I understand that the matter will be further dealt with by the Minister of Customs after he has had time to inquire into it; and it would be unfair to lay too much stress on the incident narrated by my hon. friend from Lunenburg, who I am sure has not overstated the case while there is perhaps no county so greatly interested in the fishing as the county of Lunenburg, still it is of very general interest in the province of Nova Scotia, and I think the Minister of Customs would do well to facilitate as much as possible the business of the fishermen around our coasts, and obviate if possible a repetition of such an occurrence.

speechtext: Is there any provision for the increase of the salaries of Toronto letter-carriers ? The hon. minister promised the other night to bring down some information respecting the salaries paid to the letter-carriers, and the number -who had taken advantage of the provisions of his Bill.

The minister read a list of those who are to receive increases in the Halifax post office. To whom does he intend to give increases in the Toronto post office ?

In view of the statement of the. minister that the inspector is going to Winnipeg in a few days, I take this opportunity to draw the attention of the Postmaster General to the very serious complaints that are being made in Winnipeg and in the west generally with respect to the post office service. In the city of Winnipeg the way the post office business is being transacted amounts now to almost a public scandal. It is entirely inadequate and the only explanation we can offer is that the department at Ottawa does not appreciate the tremendous increase in the volume of business that is monthly taking place in the west. I understood the minister to say on Friday afternoon, that a sorting room was going to be provided when the Canadian Pacific Railway Company erect a new station, but that question has been hanging fire for two years and it looks now as if there will be no new station for another year. The congestion in the Win-

600S
nipeg post office is such that delay of that kind cannot be tolerated. They will simply have to put the mail matter into the lane instead of in the building. Some of the departments of the local post oflice are in a disgraceful condition. If the minister inquires he will find that there is no room in the dead letter oflice for the clerks to sit to do their work, and they have to sit on bags to do the sorting. The conditions are not sanitary there, and are positively injurious. Some plan must be found to properly man the post office. Not less than five left the service there at the end of last month. I was in the post office myself a short time ago, and I found that ini the registry department the work is being done by temporary employees who are classed as labourers. That does not look safe. If the men are fit for the service, their work ought be properly appreciated. I believe that two-thirds of the mail matter that goes through the Winnipeg office is sorted in the boxes. The letter carrier service has not met the requirements of the city and the'peopie have found it necessary to have boxes. There are six persons working at these boxes and only one of them has been in the employment of the department for a year. It is impossible for them to understand their work and the result is all kinds of misplaced mails. There are more complaints than there are officers to attend to them. It does seem that the service is growing worse and worse. With the great influx of population at the present time !t would look as if the service is going to break down altogether unless some radical improvement is made. I understand that there are often as many as 2,000 changes of address by temporary residents in Winnipeg in a month. There is no officer told off to attend to that work, so that this mail matter gets laid to one side and accumulates unassorted and undelivered. I know ns a matter of fact that the staff are working overtime, and the reason that it is not increased is the fear that the employees would resign in greater numbers than ever.
I wonder if the hon. Postmaster General knows the number of resignations that have taken place in the Winnipeg post office since the beginning of this year. I know that there have been so many that the work of tlie office is crippled, and I would like to know, and the citizens would like to know, whether any plan has been outlined for carrying on the business of the office and organizing the staff so that not only the present work, but the increased work which is bound to press upon the office from this lime forth, will be kept up.

The Winnipeg post office building is wholly ininadequate to the requirements of the office and it will not be possible to put that office on a proper footing until additions are made to the building or some of the other gov-

eminent staff are removed so that we can have additional accommodation in that building. The architect of the Public Works Department has already been at Winnipeg along with the chief superintendent of the post office, plans for the remodelling of the building have been prepared and approved of, and everything awaits the vote of parliament to give us money to proceed with the work. The staff of the Winnipeg post office, so far as its numbers go, is perfectly adequate. The city has made great progress of late, and the business of the office has outgrown the capacity of the building. The hon. gentleman has alluded to temporary employees. There is no temporary employee in the Winnipeg post office who is legally qualified for 'permanent appoint-) ment. There are not in that young country as many persons who have passed the civil service examination as are required from time to time, and consequently it is necessary to appoint persons temporarily until they can pass the examination and be legally appointed on the permanent staff. That is the only reason why so many temporary employees are in the Winnipeg post office at the present time. I do not say that the service is sufficient; quite the contrary. I am as well aware as my hon. friend is, that it is not sufficient, and I am as anxious as he is to make it sufficient. But it cannot be made sufficient in advance of the necessary accommodation being provided. The difficulty to-day arises from the great prosperity of Winnipeg, and the west, which has thrown a much greater population into the city, and has consequently increased the work of the post office. With reference to the money-order and registration branches, it is part of the plan of re-organization to transfer these to the upper part of the building, and that will be done as soon as the upper part of the building can be prepared to receive them. When those two branches are removed from the lower part of the building, more accommodation will be afforded for the general business of the office. But even all this is but a make-sliift, as I understand it, and the government will have to supply additional building accommodation at the city of Winnipeg at an early date.

I am glad to see that the minister appreciates the situation. It is no worse than either he or I have explained to the House; it is simply very serious. But the question is, is it going to be remedied at once, or is it going to be allowed to get worse ? Because it seems to me that if some improvement is not effected more quickly than is usually the case with government departments, there will be soon a congestion in the office which it will be difficult to overcome. As regards the staff, it may be that there are persons there who are not qualified to be appointed permanently. The office is manned by persons em-

ployed temporarily, many of tliem being rated as labourers. For this some remedy should speedily be found. People who have gone In during last year have left because the salary has not been sufficient to induce them to remain. Five left during the past month, and at present there are but few competent employees, for want of experience. How does the lion. Postmaster General expect to remedy this state of affairs, and remedy it in time to be of some use ?

There have been several experienced post office men sent from the east to Winnipeg post office within the last few weeks. The staff is to-day adequate for the work, but it cannot do its work properly until sufficient accommodation is supplied. The work will be done under great disadvantages until then. I have no doubt that in a short time parliament will be asked to provide for additional building accommodation, and the sooner we reach those estimates and get them passed the sooner the work will be undertaken.

Did I understand the hou. Postmaster General to say that the reason why there are so many temporary employees in the Winnipeg post office is because he could not And men who had passed the civil service examination? Is that right ?
Yes.
Might I ask the bon. minister if that same difficulty is experienced in Ontario and other provinces ?
There is no trouble of that kind in other parts of Canada east of Winnipeg. It may be found to some slight extent in British Columbia, but there is not the same rapid increase of population there.
Is there any insuperable difficulty in the way of having extra examinations by civil service commissioners ?
The Civil Service Act provides that the examinations shall be held only annually, I think in the month of November.

Might I inquire of the lion. Postmaster General if his attention has been called to the fact that the cost of living is very much greater in Winnipeg than in eastern cities, and does he think he can get the work done in the Winnipeg post office at the same wages as are paid in the east ?
No, 1 do not.
What does the bon. Postmaster General propose to do about it ?
They are paid more in Winnipeg than in eastern cities.

I might explain to the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Kemp) that the employees in Winnipeg get $10 a month more than they do in the east; but even that is inadequate ; and the reason we have so few on the permanent list is that they will not stay in the office long enough to be appointed. Forty dollars a month is less than a man can live on. and they are constantly leaving. The better ones leave first, so that the inferior ones are left. To run the office properly, it is necessary to have efficient people, and you can only have them by paying as good salaries as are paid elsewhere. Those who have left have done so because the express companies and others are offering higher salaries than are paid in the post office.
Ten dollars a month does not more than cover the extra house rent in Winnipeg today in comparison with this city or any other eastern city. Ten dollars a month is not adequate, and the proof is they are leaving the postal service in spite of the inducement of permanent employment and gradual increase. The pay is too low at the start. Unless a man has been five years on the staff he will leave, and it is the best and most promising who are leaving first.

Apparently the Post Office Department is in some respects in as bad a position as the Militia Department. The hon. gentleman says that the position of the letter-carriers has been much improved under his new Bill. He has not however made that quite clear. If there has been any improvement, it is very extraordinary that only fifteen or sixteen have taken advantage of the new law.

I do not know where the hon. gentleman got his information that only fifteen had availed themselves of the new law. I stated that 195 old employees had come under the new system. One hundred and ninety-five letter-carriers have elected to come under that system, and I have no doubt that when the Bill now before the Senate becomes law, a very much larger number will avail themselves of it. The time allowed to take advantage of the new system had expired. A good many of them had not time to fully appreciate the benefits and have since intimated their desire to come under the new law. To meet this desire, a clause has been inserted in the Bill, which passed this House and is now before the Senate, extending the time for admission. My hon. friend will then be able to judge whether these people appreciate the advantages of the new law or not. If my hon. friend desires to know how the matter stands, I will give him a few figures and he can judge for himself. The transfers from the old to the new sys-

tern were made at irregular dates. Tlie letter-carriers could come in whenever they liked within six months, and therefore I cannot give a tabulated statement running a clear year, but I can give you a number of figures which will explain the advantages of the new system. I have here a statement showing the effect of the change regarding a hundred and ninety-five letter-carriers.
Were they drawing the maximum salary ?
Some of them were.
How many-fifteen or sixteen '!
I think I said fifteen.
That is all of those receiving the maximum salary who have taken advantage of the new law ?
These are some figures showing the actual salaries paid to certain letter-carriers and what they would have received under the old law.
Give us the dates of the appointments of those gentlemen ?

Mr. Britnell, appointed 11th September, 1S99, would have received under the old law $435, and since his transfer he is receiving $4(14.50, and will be entitled to a bonus of $20, making an increase of $49.50 over what he would have received had he remained under the old system.
What about his superannuation ?
It is not affected by the change. He is entitled to all the rights regarding superannuation.
What is the length of the holidays received under the old system and under the new ?

My hon. friend is so curious that he will not allow me to give the information. I propose to answer the first question first and then will come to the others. The hon. gentleman evidently does not wish me to make good my statement that a certain number of letter-carriers, who had elected to come under the new system, were substantial gainers by the transfer.
The hon. minister knows that he is only advancing his own friends.
The hon. gentleman does not wish to have this information but probably the committee would desire it.
Delighted to have it.

The best possible evidence that the men are not satisfied with his legislation, and believe it is of no substantial benefit to them, is the fact that only fifteen in the whole Dominion have availed of its provisions. Under the old system a man entered at $360, and he was increased by $30 or $40 a year till he reached the maximum of $600. Under the old system the men were paid during sickness, they got three weeks holidays and they got superannuation when they retired from the service. Under the new system they commence with $1.25 a day, and in four of five years they reach $2, or if they have been placed in grade E afterwards they receive $2.25, but their holidays have been cut down, they receive no pay when they are sick, and when they retire or are dismissed from the service they only get their own contributions into the fund. Although he does not stand quite so well in respect to super-annnuation, a man whose wages have been increased to $1,000 in nine years has a fund in reserve much larger than he could hope to receive from the superannuation fund. The only important question to consider here is whether a man getting $626 a year is well paid for his services. We must take into consideration the character and quality of the men who carry on the business of letter-carriers. I do not want to say a word against the characters of the men ; but the qualification necessary to a successful letter-carrier are simply physical strength and the ability to read the address on a letter. That class of men are not scarce. In the ordinary avocations of life they would regard themselves as receiving a princely salary were they getting $626 a year, especially when we consider that the time they labour amounts to a little over eight hours per day. Now, I am quite satisfied that there is not an employer of labour in this House who is paying labouring men more than $2 per day. The position of a letter-carrier is such that when a vacancy occurs a hundred men are after it. They are willing to leave their jobs as moulders, machinists, brick-layers, carpenters or any of the ordinary avocations of life. They are willing to drop the trowel at once and become letter-carriers at $626, a year, with two weeks holidays, two suits of clothes, and shoes, amounting to $40 a year more. I asked a motorman to-day what wages he was getting. He said $1.65 for ten hours labour. The letter-carriers get $2 a day and work two hours a day less, and do work requiring no higher degree of intelligence than the motorman. Considering this service fairly, I think that a letter-carrier who is getting $2 a day is getting as much money as he could hope to obtain in any other walk of life requiring no greater degree of intelligence and training. Several deputations have since waited on the acting minister, and I think it would be a gracious act on his part to carry out the promise made by the Postmaster General. The letter-carriers are a very deserving class of men and certainly have presented a case that is well worthy of consideration*

My hon. colleague, the Postmaster General, had taken the matter into consideration before he left, and had practically devised a scheme by which these men

would be given an increase. I had two or three deputations ot the letter-carriers wait on me. There was some difference of opinion as to the best plan to be adopted, and after full consideration I concluded it was best to allow it to stand over until next session. I think that the letter-carriers themselves were pretty well satisfied also to have the question remain over. While I am not in a position to say what will be done, I can assure my hon. friend that the Postmaster General and the government are favourable to an increase, and that a plan will be adopted which will, I trust, meet, the views of the letter-carriers and the House generally.

I understand, from what the acting Postmaster General has said, that a plan had been drafted and that that plan had been submitted to the carriers themselves, who waited on the acting minister, and that the reason it was not put into effect is because there was difference of opinion among the letter-carriers as to the best method of carrying it into effect. Is that correct ?

Not quite. We discussed different plans, and after full consideration it was thought better to leave the matter stand over until next session. It was' late in the session and there was a great deal to do. And I think that the letter-carriers themselves were satisfied that it would be in their interest to let the matter stand until next session.
I think that is pretty strong evidence that a pledge was given the letter-carriers by the gentleman who was acting for the Postmaster General, which pledge was no doubt made with his approval. That is the justification I had for making the statement I did.

The hon. gentleman has read from ' Hansard ' some observations made in the discussion arising out of a question put by the senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett). It is true that a deputation waited upon me in the department in the spring of 1901. A number of members were present, including my hon. colleague the Finance Minister, and, if my memory does not deceive me, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition was there also. I was leaving for Australia the next day, and after hearing all that could be advanced, I said that various plans were under consideration, that I had not matured anything definite, but that if I did before I left, I would give the benefit of my views to my hon. colleague the Minister of Finance, who was going to look after the Post Office Department in my absence. I gave him the benefit of my views, but after consideration I wrote him that I thought it would be better to let the matter stand until another year. Accordingly it was allowed to stand until last year, when the government did introduce a measure which has met with the approval of 195 letter-carriers and will doubtless meet with the approval of the very large majority ; and in addition there is another measure before this parliament, which will give them a further increase of $TS a year, or about 12 per cent. All who choose may take advantages of these very substantial advances, but no' definite plan was ever announced to any one and nothing definite promised. The first time any definite promise was made was when I introduced a Bill last session, which has been supplemented by another Bill this session.

Mr. Sloan, who is a railway mail clerk, met with an accident. Since then he has not been able to be on the road. This is simply a small balance, I suppose,-owing to him up to the time of the accident. We put him into some light work inside.

The hon. Postmaster General, some years ago, made some arrangement about promoting clerks. A clerk temporarily in the service and desiring a permanent appointment, would have to accept a reduced salary for a time. There

were a number of clerks In 1896, when the Postmaster General came into office, who were temporarily appointed.
Appointed under my administration ?

No ; the hon. minister took good care that his own friends were appointed permanently. They were clerks who were employed in the temporary service when the hon. gentleman came into office. Are any of these still temporary clerks ?

I am informed that at the time this government took office there were a number of temporary employees, railway mail clerks. Under the law, as it was then, if they had been made permanent they would have had to begin at the initial salary of their class. But the law was changed in 1898, and we made them all permanent, giving them the salary they were receiving at the time of their permanent appointment.

I believe I can say, speaking for a number of my constituents, that the substantial measure of justice that has been given to the letter-carriers and railway mail clerks and other employees of the outside service has been received with a great deal of gratitude on their part. And, no doubt, if an opportunity is afforded, as I hope it will be, they will strongly express their gratitude. While discussing the matter of increases for the mail clerks, the letter-carriers and the outside service of the Post Office Department, I wish to submit to the committee reasons which will be applicable to the Post Office Department, and also to the civil service generally. I crave your permission, Mr. Chairman, 'to lay before the committee certain figures and statements in connection with the civil service generally which. I think, ought to receive the close attention of the members of this committee. I want to submit to you that the time has come when the salaries of the civil service ought to be increased all round. It seems to me that, owing to the great changes which have taken place in Canada, particularly within the last few years, the time has come when, for the reasons which I shall have the honour to mention, the salaries of the civil service generally ought to be increased. If one examines the work now being done in the various departments, one is struck at once with the fact that the civil servants of to-day are performing a great deal more work and giving a great deal more of their time to the country than they did formerly. There has been a very substantial increase in the quantity of their duties and a change in the nature and extent of those duties. There has been also, as every one knows, a very great increase in the cost of living. I do not know that this increase has been greater in the city that I represent than in any other city in Canada, but

I am able to say that it has in larger ratio than in a great many other cities. We have to pay more for rent, wages, fuel, municipal rates, food, clothing-in fact, all the commodities, all the comestibles, have largely increased all over the country, and particular}* in the cities. The cost of living to-day, I think, may be said to have increased 35 or 40 per cent over what it was twenty-five or thirty years ago. The wage-earners all over the world are demanding and receiving to-day a much larger wage than they received a few years ago. Mechanics are better paid, farmers get a better return for their labour, the professions receive larger fees, teachers, professors and, I believe, clergymen also, are in receipt of much larger- stipends than even a few years ago. These matters are all decided by comparison. If one looks at what has taken place in the banks, the railway companies, the insurance companies,' and all the great corporations which do the financial, commercial and industrial work of the community, he finds that the salaries of the principal officers and of all their employees from top to bottom have been very largely increased within the last few years. I wish also to give yon some figures which will show how much the increase of salaries is justified, how much, in fact, it is demanded, by the place that Canada now occupies and the attention she is receiving from the 'world at large, in order to make the stipends paid to our state officials commensurate with the dignity of the nation. I take the year 1S73 as a basis of comparison, because that is the time when the rate of salaries in the civil service was fixed ; and it is well to remember that in the thirty years since then there has been no increase in the salaries of the civil service, while every other occupation in Canada has expected and has received a return for its labour increased, in some cases by 50 or 75, or even 100 per cent. In 1873 the total revenue of Canada was $20,000,000: in 1902-and probably it is more in 1903-it was $60,000,000. In 1873 we had 5,000 miles of railway ; to-day the country has 20.000 miles of railway. In 1873, in the Post Offic Department, now presided over by the hon. member for North York (Hon. Now if we take the heads of the civil service we find that they were receiving more in 1873 than they are now. They are receiving, the most of them $3,200, some of them, I believe, receive $3,500. and one something over $4,000, the deputy Minister of Railways and Canals. Now these deputy heads of departments have a very much greater responsibility: owing to the circumstances I have mentioned and to many other reasons, their duties have much increased, both in kind, in quantity and importance. They are brought before the public, not only in our own country, but in other countries,

in the discharge of their official duties. They have been sent abroad on many occasions to represent the government of Canada, and in fact have great responsibilities cast upon them. I say therefore that because of their duties having been so much increased these gentlemen should receive consideration at the hands of this parliament and receive an increase of salary. When ?

Probably the hon. gentleman, being a lawyer, knows how to twist words. He is trying to convey the impression that I said that some of these officials were worse off than they were some years ago. I made no such statement.
If the hon. gentleman did not mean that

My hon. friend is not a lawyer, but he can twist a statement much better than many lawyers.

I suppose I ought to feel proud at the compliment paid me by a gentleman of the ability of the hon. member for Ottawa. Did I hear the hon. gentleman aecurately in understanding him to say that the cost of living has increased during the past twenty-five years by 35 per cent ?

I said that in the last thirty years the cost of living in cities had increased 30 per cent, 35 per cent, and in some cases, 40 per cent. But whether my hon. friend made the statement I credited him with or not, the figures are there to prove that the want of liberality has been the other way. In 1882 the secretaries of departments were receiving $2,800. The secretary had an assistant who was in receipt of $2,000. To-day the maximum salary to which the secretary can aspire is $2,400; whilst in 1878, when the political friends of the hon. member came into power and for a few years thereafter, they were receiving $2,800, that is, $400 more. I cannot exactly remember the date, but I think that Was changed in 1889 or 1900, by the Conservative government, when $400 was taken away from the secretary of the department and the post of assistant secretary was abolished. The secretary is now replaced by a chief clerk whose salary is $1,850. That was the work of a government which the hon. gentleman supported. Then the accountant of the department in those days was receiving $2,800, and had a cashier at $2,200, and an assistant accountant' at '$2,200. To-day the maximum of the accountant is $2,400, as against $2,200. Both the cashier and the assistant accountant have been abolished and replaced by clerks' whose salary only reaches $1,800. The accountant to-day is only in receipt of $2,000. The chief superintendent of the savings bank received, in 1882, $2,700, and the assistant was paid $1,775. The highest the superintendent can new attain is $2,400, with no assistant. The salary of the present superintendent is about $1,900, $800 less than in 1882. Certainly some of the figures show that the Liberals have been more generous than their predecessors in the treatment of the officials. Again I repeat that these are relative questions which are decided by means of comparisons, and I think it is by

looking at tlie figures in tlie various departments that \re can arrive at a correct judgment as to whether the civil servants today are iu receipt of the salaries to whicn they are entitled by reason of their services and by reason of the conditions which I have described. Take the Tost Office Department. We find that in 1896, the year in which there was a change of government, there were employed in the Post Office Department 254 clerks, of whom 19S were permanent and fifty-six temporary. The revenue in that year was $4,005,890. In 1902, with a revenue of $5,128,118, there were 279 employed in the Post Office Department of whom 208 were permanent and seventy-one temporary. It will be seen at once that with a revenue of $1,250,000 less than what it is now there were only twenty-five employees less in the Post Office Department, or to put it the other way, with a revenue of $4,000,000, we had 254 clerks while with a revenue of $5,250,000, we have 279 clerks, or an increase of only twenty-five in six years.
Wbat does that prove ?
That proves that the civil service to-day are doing much more work than they were doiug during the period of the former government.
Does that apply to letter-carriers ?
No, I did not pretend to say that it did. I am speaking of the civil service generally. I am not dealing with the letter-carriers. I thought my hon. friend had enough of the letter-carriers.
I thought it would include them. I thought the hon. gentleman was harping back to them.

Since 1896 the Post office Department has established a branch known as the postal note branch and to man that fifteen clerks were taken from the departmental staff. Since then five clerks were added to the staff of the branch. The point which I have been endeavouring to make and which must be plain to my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke), who generally follows a discussion with such keen interest as not to miss the point, is that we have now only twenty-five employees more in the Post Office Department, while one-fifth more work is being done. I am not dealing with letter-carriers, but with the post office inside service. If we look outside of Canada at the other British colonies, and I think this is a fair test to apply in matters of this kind, what do we find ? We find in three of the British colonies the figures of which I have looked at, the following results :	In New South Wales, with a
population of 1,356,000, the deputy heads have an average salary of $4,800 each ; in Victoria, with a population of 1,163.000, the deputy heads have a salary of $4,252, and

in Cape Colony, with a population of 1,-
527,000,	the deputv heads have a salary of $4,742, whilst in Canada, with a population of 6,000,000, the average salary of a deputy minister is $3,200.
Why does the government not increase the salary ?

That is what I want them to do. I submit the time has come, when, notwithstanding the fact that a number of people throughout the community believe that the civil servants are already well enough paid, we must really consider the matter. We must remember what I said before, that this rate of salary has not been touched for thirty years. While speaking of the civil servants, I want to refer also to a matter which has very often worried me not only here, but abroad. For instance, when in England or in France or United States, I was asked the question what the salary of our Prime Minister was and what the salaries of our other ministers were and what the salaries of our judges were, I confess I felt a deal of shame when I had to admit that the Prime Minister of Canada was paid the paltry sum of $8,000, that the salaries of the other ministers were $7,000, and that the salaries of our judges were $5,000. There is not one single British colony which pays its officers as little as we pay. I had hoped the time would come when parliament, for the sake of its dignity, for the sake of Canada, and for the sake of the place it occupies in the eyes of the world, would have thought it proper of its own motion to have increased the salary of the Prime Minister of the country to such a substantial sum as would not cause shame to any of us when asked what the salary of the Prime Minister was. I think these remarks apply not only to the Prime Minister, but to the other ministers also. They apply to the judges and I hope also, when the House considers this question, it will consider the propriety of affording the leader of the opposition, who sacrifices his time, his profession and his dearest interests, some recognition of the claims which he has upon the country. I say the time has come when, because of the changed conditions in the country, because of the greater duties which the civil servants have to perform, because of the increased cost of living, because of the greater demands in money matters which are made upon them and in the face of the great prosperity which exists, in face of the higher salaries which are being paid to managers and the employees of the greater corporations, we must meet the question fairly and squarely and afford our civil servants and the servants of the state a remuneration which is commensurate with their services, commensurate with their requirements and commensurate with the dignity, honour and position which Canada now occupies in the eyes of the world.

I am sure the committee will be somewhat gratified at the admirable election speech which the bon. gentleman has just made. It is quite easy to see that we now seem to be on the brink of a general election. That bon. gentleman has been moved to tears almost over the civil servants in Ottawa.

I have almost every session, since I have been in this House, on some occasion or other when there was not an election in sight, said something on behalf of my constituents, including the members of the civil service.

As occasion arose evening after evening in this House when the government were endeavouring to make a name for themselves by depriving those gentlemen who were the hon. gentlemen's constituents of their statutory increases, I heard no strong appeals from him.
The hon. gentleman could not have been in the House then, because I did appeal on two or three occasions.

The hon. gentleman says he did appeal on two or three occasions out of several thousands that have liap-jiened since I have had the honour of being a member of this House. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Belcourt) remarked that many people in Canada thought that the civil servants were well enough paid, if not
overpaid. Let me tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Belcourt) that his political friends made it a campaign cry against the Conservative party that the members of the civil service were overpaid and under worked, and if the impression which he speaks of, prevails in the country then it is due to the efforts of his party friends that that impression prevails. I do not know whether the deputy heads receive too much or too little, but, I say that any official that has not the maximum of his class is entitled by law and contract to get his annual increase, and it is nothing to the credit of the government that these increases have been stopped. Let me appeal to the Postmaster General on behalf of the rural postmasters of this country who are undoubtedly underpaid. It may be that he can get others to discharge the service for the same pay, and it may be that under our system we cannot give them full and fair remuneration, but he certainly should make some effort to place their pay on a fairly reasonable basis. I wish to ask the Postmaster General if it is his intention at the present session to make increases all around in the pay of the country postmasters.

The postmasters are being paid to-day according to the same scale that was in force when we took office. If it should be decided at any time to alter that scale they will at once be notified. I stated in committee on Friday night-and I assume my hon. friend was not present-that legislation is not necessary to increase the salaries of postmasters other than those postmasters who are on the civil service list. Under the Post Office Act it remains with the Postmaster General to increase the salaries of the others so that legislation is not necessary.

I am as wise now as I was before. I did not ask the Postmaster General what the scale formerly was. We have been told by his supporter (Mr. Belcourt) that the cost of living has increased from 30 to 40 per cent and the Postmaster General evidently pays no attention to that statement.

I heard my hon. friend (Mr. Belcourt) say that that increase extended over 30 years. Perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) can tell for what portion of that 30 years the Conservative government is responsible that they would not increase the salaries of the postmasters on account of the increased cost of living.
Mi-. CLANCY. The hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) has been in the House for seven years and he never made the discovery until recently that the cost of living had so much increased. The Postmaster General has been seven years at the head of his department and he has not been able

to make up his mind yet as to whether the postmasters are paid too low salaries or not. He tells us that they will be notified when their salaries will be increased. I do not think the Postmaster General weighed his words when he said that. Did he think he was enlightening the House with such a statement ? He ought to be able to state from his seat as a minister whether he thinks the postmasters are sufficiently paid, and if they are not sufficiently paid that he will increase their salaries. I was not here the other evening, but I am told that the Postmaster General boasted that notwithstanding that the rate of postage had been materially reduced the revenue had gone up on account of the increased business.
I did not allude to it.

Perhaps I was misinformed as to that. The bon. gentleman would scarcely deny that he has said over and over again in the country that there had been a material reduction in the burdens of the people and a very substantial increase in the revenue. I do not know whether he is now prepared to recede from that position and admit that it is not the ease. The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that the burdens on the people are greater now than they were in the matter of postage. The hon. gentleman, it is true, decreased the letter postage from three cents to two cents, but he has increased the postage on the other classes of second, third and fourth class matter, in some respects 100 per cent; and he has put this increased burden upon the class who are least able to bear it. Who are the people who, after all, benefit by the reduction in the postage from three to two cents ? It is not the taxpayer generally, but it is a few persons in the great business centres. Who are the class who make up for that ? The men who scarcely write two letters a year, but who use the mails to carry parcels of every description. I will give the hon. gentleman some instances of his splendid reductions and of the ways he has lightened the burdens of the people. Formerly newspapers were free for all distances in Canada ; now they are free only within a radius of twenty miles. Newspapers and periodicals posted at a place other than the place of publication were charged one cent for four ounces : now the hon. gentleman has them at one cent for two ounces, or an increase of 100 per cent. Newspapers, single copies, weighing not more than one ounce, were formerly charged half a cent each ; now they are charged one cent. Books, printed, of instruction, music, dra-wings, and other such books, were charged one cent for four ounces ; this has been increased to one cent for two ounces, or an increase of 100 per cent. Pamphlets, circulars, handbills, packages of seeds, plants, grafts and similar mail matter, were charged one cent for four ounces ; the post-Mr. CLANCY.
age is now one cent for two ounces, or an increase of 100 per cent. On maps, printing, drawings, lithographs, photographs, sheet music, deeds, wills, mortgages, chattel mortgages, insurance policies, voters' lists, assessment rolls, municipal returns, patterns, samples of merchandise, of which there are thousands pass through the mails daily, the hon. gentleman found the postage at one cent for two ounces, and doubled that by charging two cents for four ounces, this being the minimum on which the charge is made, which is an increase of 100 per cent. I might continue the list, but I have given the classes of mail matter on which the hon. gentleman has doubled up the rates. Then take the trade that is going on through the mails. The poorer classes of the people, from Halifax on one side to Vancouver on the other, go to the large cities of the province of Ontario, and some to Montreal, and pay this rate of postage on parcels of merchandise sent from these places to persons who use the mails for the purpose of getting these goods. The hon. gentleman has been able to take the burden of postage largely from one class of people and lay it on another class who do not use the mails except from dire necessity. These are fair samples of what a public benefactor the hon. gentleman has proved himself to be. He has starved the service in a most scandalous manner. Now. Sir, there was formerly a fair growth of post offices in this country during a period of great depression. I am going to call the hon. gentleman's attention to the number of post offices and the service he is giving the people during the period of expansion which we have been enjoying for some j'ears. The number of post offices in existence in 1890 was 7,913 : the number in existence in 1S90 was 9.103, an increase in six years of 1,190. That was during a period of very great depression, when the necessities of the country did not demand the increase that they did at a later date, when you would expect at least a corresponding increase. Now, what has been the hon. gentleman's record ? In 1902 the number of post offices w-as 9,958, or an increase of 855, as against an increase of 1,190 for the same period previously. How does the hon. gentleman account for that discrepancy? Does he mean to say that the people were so well supplied with post offices by the former government that he did not need to increase the number ? But I am told that it is almost impossible to wring a new post office from the hon. gentleman. He is always frightened that it will interfere with his revenue-with his surplus, as an hon. friend suggests. He would be very flattered to be told that he has a surplus ; but he has not a surplus. If the hon. gentleman is able to give the country a good service and to show a better balance on the credit side than has been shown in former years, he only does it to the extent to which he starves the service. But with the country growing as

it is at present, and with the immense territory of which Canada is made up, no Postmaster General can give a good service and at the same time show a credit balance. So the hon. gentleman has been driven to the rather discreditable device of concealing his accounts by showing to the public only a portion of the service. The hon. gentleman did that no doubt with the avowed object of showing how he had made the two sides of the ledger balance. Speaking for myself, I do not think this House or this country would expect any apology from the hon. gentleman, so long as he gave the country a good service, whether it paid its way or not. He has taken it off one class and put it on another, and to-day the public are paying more postage than before. The rate in 1896 was 93 cents per head, and today it is 96 cents per head, after all this pretended reduction. I know of no more conclusive evidence to show the fraud which the hon. gentleman is perpetrating on the people when pretending that he is lessening their burdens.
