Mi'. JOHNSTON (Cardwell). The first session I was here I asked the hon. Postmaster General to do something, if possible, for the country post office keepers, and he promised he would try. The salaries of these men amount to from $15 to $20 and even less.
In fact the neighbours, who get their letters in these little offices, have to club together and pay fifty cents or $1 apiece in order to get the postmasters to keep the offices. I have listened to a great deal of information about the arrangements made for the benefit of the letter-carriers in the cities and towns and also for improving the positions of the postmasters there, who have their caretakers and are supplied with light and fuel, but I have yet to hear of anything being done for the poor country postmasters, who have to keep longer hours than do the men in the cities and towns, and who are not paid enough to heat their little offices. It is pretty hard that a country post office has to be run at a loss because the government will not supply the postmaster with sufficient wage to pay his running expenses. Were it not for the contributions of the neighbours, many of these post offices would have to be closed. The hon. gentleman has boasted of having given us a 2-cent rate, but that has had the effect of reducing the revenue in the country post offices and consequently of reducing the emoluments of the postmasters, so that the change is altogether against their interests. Three years ago the hon. gentleman asked me what I wished to have done and what suggestion I could make that would enable these men to be better paid and not run the department into debt. 1 made a suggestion, which I think a reasonable one, that in the cities and towns, where postmasters are paid $1,600 $1,700 a year and are furnished with fuel, light and a caretaker, they might be made to do with less and our country postmasters in the rural districts, even if it be only farmers who are served, the sum of $50 each for taking care of their little offices. If the hon. gentleman cannot do otherwise, let him take the money off the cities and add it to the rural districts.

Let me first inform the hon. gentleman that the reduction in the rate of postage has in no case led to any reduction in the salaries of the postmasters. When that reduction took place instructions were issued that there was to be no reduction in the salaries of the postmasters, even if the revenue should be reduced. The hon. gentleman suggests that there should be an increase of $50 to each country postmaster
Not an increase, but that at least $50 be paid to each.

A minimum of $50. That is not a new question. This same question has come up periodically for the last forty years. I heard it a great many times when I was on the other side, and the answer given then was what I must give my hon. friend now. Those small offices, to which my hon. friend alludes, are

not such as can be expected to supply a living to the incumbents. They are established merely to suit the convenience of groups of people. In fact, wherever there are a dozen people in a district, a post office is given them, even if it is within a short distance of an adjoining post office. It is a rare thing to refuse to establish a post office because of its close proximity to another, say within a mile or two. If the immediate neighbourhood desires it, the post office is given, but the result of the multiplication of these offices must be to diminish the revenue of each. The policy of multiplying these offices is a good one because it adds greatly to the conveniences of the people, and the postmasters enjoy some advantages besides the pay. For instance, they have the special advantage of getting their mail brought to their house, and I do not suppose that the salary can be considered as any remuneration. The salaries were not fixed by me, but are such as I found them fixed by my predecessors and confirmed by long usage. As to whether it is possible to increase them by giving each country postmaster $50 a year, that would mean a very considerable increase in our expenditure. It would mean an increase of $35 per year to each country postmaster. The number of increases would be very great. It would be rash for me to estimate the number, but perhaps it would not be out of the way to suppose it would require $100,000 to give an increase of $35 per head to the class of postmasters t-o whom the lion gentleman refers. So, while it does not seem much to suggest that an increase of $35 be given to a particular person, yet to give such an increase to all in that class involves a good deal of expenditure. Therefore, the proposition should not be entered upon lightly. The hon. member for Bothwell alluded to the increased rate, and suggested, amongst other things, that the people who purchased newspapers had to pay higher subscription rates because of it. I do not know to what case he alludes, but I myself have not heard of any instance where subscription rates have been increased because of the imposition of postage upon newspapers. But whether increased or not the imposition of rates on newspapers was, I think, justifiable. Parliament thought it was, and so made the increase. The hon. member from Bothwell says the reduction of the letter rate proved a benefit to none except to those in industrial centres. I do not admit the soundness of that proposition. Every man, be he a resident of an industrial centre or of a rural district, and no matter what be his walk of life, if he uses the post office at all, then to the extent that he uses it, he is benefited. The advantage of the lower rates of the letter postage are rateably distributed among the population in proportion as they make use

of the post office. I doubt very much if the great mass of the people of Canada, would if they could, return to the old rate. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) has a policy of that kind, if he would like to go back to the former rate, and would test the opinion of the House, we could have an interesting debate; and, if the majority favour the return to the three cent rate, that rate will come into effect, and the hon. gentleman will be able to feel that he has rendered a very distinguished service to the people in imposing great burdens upon them. The hon. gentleman speaks of increases in the rates in certain third and fourth class matter. The rate on merchandise passing through the post office is the same as when I took office. I have not changed that rate at all. The rate was one cent per ounce then, and it is one cent per ounce now. There were some changes made in some minor matters, the volume of which is very trifling comparatively. Ninety per cent of all the postal revenue is from letters alone, and the postage paid on these extra articles of mail matter to which the hon. gentleman alludes are comparatively trifling, so far as any effect on the revenue is concerned. Nevertheless, the present rates ai-e as low as they are in any place in the world. They are the same as those charged in the United States; and, I think that the Canadian rates on the classes of matter to which the hon. gentleman refers, are as low as in England, although our area is so much greater.

If the hon. minister will turn to his own report and compare it with the postal guides of 1896, he will find that the statement I have made is absolutely correct. Take, for instance, the first item here. ' Books printed, books of instruction, music books, drawing books,' were one cent for four ounces, they are now one cent for two ounces. Is that a correct statement ?
That, is the rate throughout the United States.
That is not the question I asked.
What is the hon. gentleman's question ?
I will read it again. * Printed books, books of instruction, music books and drawing books,' formerly one cent for four ounces, now one cent for two ounces. Will the hon. gentleman deny that ?
I will let the hon. gentleman finish his piece-
I have asked the hon. minister a question in a courteous way. He said he did not increase the rates-

No. I did not make any such an observation.
air. CLANCY. Well, we will take the next item. ' Single copies of newspapers,

weighing not more than one ounce.' ' W hen the hon. gentleman came into office these paid one-half cent each; the charge at the present time is one cent each.
There has been no change on single newspapers.
The change appears in the postal guide and the hon. minister had better not speak from memory. But if the postal guide is not correct the hon. gentleman himself is responsible.
The secretary of the department informs me that there has been no change in the rate on single copies of newspapers since this government came into office.

Well, whether the change has been made or not, it appears in the postal guide. Now, take 1 pamphlets, circulars; seeds and plants,' the rate was one cent for four ounces, the present rate is one cent for two ounces-an increase of one hundred per cent. Then take the large class, ' maps, prints, drawings, lithographs, photographs, sheets of music, deeds, wills, mortgages, chattel mortgages, insurance policies, voters' lists, assessment rolls, municipal returns, patterns, samples of merchandise,' now one cent for two ounces, formerly two cents for four ounces, four ounces being the minimum. This practically doubles the rate. I take this from the guide that the hon. gentleman sent out for the instruction of the people. If he says the guide is wrong I shall have to leave it for him to settle it with his department. But the minister knows perfectly well that that class of matter of which there has been a very large increase, and which is still increasing, has gone up to the extent which I have stated. And I say that by reason of that, the reduction which the hon. gentleman has made to certain classes in this country has fallen on other classes. The hon. gentleman says that all classes are served alike by the reduction in letter postage. But any service of which a man may not be in a position to avail himself cannot be spoken of as a real advantage to him. Nor is the public service a fair one when only half the people can use the service, but all have to pay for it. I would ask the Postmaster General what the workingman has profited generally by this reduction V I will take the employees in Mr. Eaton's establishment, in his own city, and I will take the establishment itself. Who has profited by the reduction of the postage ? Why, that grfeat commercial concern has been saved thousands and thousands of dollars a year, and probably his employees do not write one letter a month. That is the effect of it. The hon. gentleman has laid down a rule that not one man in a hundred can avail himself of. The true rule is that every man should pay for the
service he gets. If a majority of the people are unable to avail themselves of it, and you give it to the minority in number, then that is not a fair service to the majority who don't use it, but who are paying for it in favour of the minority. That is the effect of the hon. gentleman's position today. If, on the other hand, the hon. gentleman was able to take off all the postage then it might be fair. But I repeat that the hon. gentleman has not only reduced the postage for the benefit of a few persons in Canada, but he has done what is worse, he has unloaded that reduction on to a class who do not use the mail except perhaps for third and fourth class matter. I am glad to know that the hon. gentleman does not dissent from my statement with regard to the increase in that matter that comes within the third and fourth class.
The POSTMASTER; GENERAL. I may explain to the hon. gentleman, as I did to the House, why the changes were made. When parliament was being asked to change the law, I explained that there were a number of different rates on mail matter, and a great deal of confusion was occasioned because, in many instances, there was difficulty in determining in which class the mail matter ought to fall. In the rapid despatch of business that law could not be really lived up to. In order to simplify the rates we removed many special rates. There were many different rates on different articles, for example lithographs and printed matter were charged differently. I cannot pretend to enter into all the niceties, but there were constant questions arising as to the class to which certain articles belonged. It was not a matter of count. When mail matter is passing through the post .one person may think it falls' in a certain class and is liable to a certain rate, and attach the necessary stamp upon it: while another postmaster may come to the conclusion that it ought to be rated differently. Then there was trouble. In order to meet the convenience of the public and to facilitate the transacting of business, we did away with these shades of difference by making the classification as it is now. The hon. gentleman says that every man should) pay for the service he gets. That is not altogether an unsound proposition. How then would he deal with the case of a man being called upon to pay for a service he does not use ? If a. man should only pay for the service he gets, that is another way of saying that he should not pay for the service he does not get. The hon. gentleman went on to argue that the poor man had no use for the post office, and yet under the old law the poor man had to pay the burden of the post office. Under the old administration to which we succeeded, there was an annual deficit of three fourths of a million dollars. Who paid that deficit ? The hon. gentleman shakes his

head. Who paid that deficit ? The poor man had to pay his share of it. The taxes have to be collected from the whole public, and under the system that the hon. gentleman seems to prefer, the poor men were taxed to pay for the mail service of the rich men. Under the present system the poor man has no deficit to pay for, and if he does chose to use the post office, he pays only two cents instead of three as formerly. I believe the poor man prefers to be called upon to pay two cents instead of three; I think he prefers not to pay a share of the three fourths of a million dollars of a deficit in the mail service of Canada. He is not now called upon to pay any such deficit, because there is none. The hon. gentleman knows that, and he must be extremely glad to know it. If the hon. gentleman, however, is desirous of restoring the three cent rate, the opportunity is open to him to present a proposition to this House to that effect. Let him have the courage to commit himseif to that view ; instead of skirmishing and harpiug, let him come out into the open like a man and make a proposition, then let him go back to Bothwell and see how the people there will approve such a retrograde step.

The hon. gentleman's friends are taking good care that I shall not go back to Bothwell, because they are taking care that there shall be no such constituency as Bothwell. So his challenge is rather an empty one. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that he has adopted a most extraordinary course of reasoning when he says that the poor man paid the deficit in the past when there was a three cent rate and now he does not pay a deficit under a two cent rate. How does a deficit arise V By reason of the revenue not being large enough to pay for the service; then there is a greater chance of a deficit. I ask the hon. gentleman, who is so willing to challenge me to take a course that he would not dare to take himself, I ask him to tell this House what lie intends to do with regard to the country postmasters. The hon. gentleman knows the answer he gave me. He had less courage then than he now enjoins me to have upon the question. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that we are not supposed to find politiees for the government. We have no responsibilities, and when the hon. gentleman throws out his challenges to this side of the House 1 want to tell him that he is not very courageous. He knows perfectly well that our responsibility is to criticise the conduct of the government, criticise it fairly and honestly, and I hope we have done so. Now the hon. gentleman has declared over and over again that he has a surplus. Does he say now that for the last year ending the 30tii of June, 1902, there was a surplus in his department, considering all the services throughout the Dominion ? Does he say Sir WILLIAM MITLOCK.
that ? I will venture to say that the hon. gentleman will not say so; while he says in an off-hand way, rolling it out, that there was a surplus and I knew it. The hon. gentleman did some juggling. I will venture to say that if the Yukon paid its way and a little more the hou. gentleman would include it. But, if the hon. gentleman finds there is any part in the service that is not paying its way he side-tracks that and he says :	I gave it in my statement, 1 will
exclude that, I will find a surplus, and I am not deceiving the public because I made some mention of that elsewhere. I will ask the hon, gentleman if this is an honourable way of treating the public ? The public will understand the hon. gentleman. The hon. gentleman is anxious for one thing and that is to appear before the country as having been a great reformer in regard to postal matters. His reforms have consisted in starving the postmasters.
We are paying them as much as they got under the former administration.

My hon. friend says they got as much under the former government. Does he mean to say that if it should appear to him now that they were not fully paid under the former .government, he is relieved from the responsibility of giving them their rights now ? The hon. gentleman is very fond of saying that he has changed matters as he found them under the former government. If that is the case why not change this ?
Everything we found was bad.

Quite so. I think the country is beginning to discover that. To give the reason that the former government, under different conditions, paid the same salaries as are paid now, is to my mind not a fair answer to the question.
Why is it not ?
I will tell the hon. gentleman why.
Yes, that would be interesting.

As the hon. gentleman beside me '(Mr. Johnston Cardwell) pointed out a moment ago the duties of postmasters have increased. There are many places where they have to serve other offices. I have a case in my mind where the postmaster getting the same salary that he got when the hon. gentleman came in has certain other post offices to attend to. His office became a distributing point for one or two other places, but he still received the same salary as he did before.

If there is any distribution work assigned to a man he is paid for it according to a regular scale, and if the hon. gentleman will give

me the name of the office to which he alludes, we will see whether there is any distribution work for which the postmaster is not being paid and if there is he will be paid for it. It does not depend upon me. The officers automatically deal with all such cases and they give the postmasters the payment they are entitled to according to the scale provided for distribution work.
That is not salary.
It is in addition to salary.
I am speaking of the increased duties that are devolving upon postmasters.
Distribution to other offices.

Quite so, but the hon. gentleman knows perfectly . well that he must be there to take these mails and that by reason of the increased duties devolving upon him the increased sum paid him for distribution is not a fair compensation for the additional time he has to give that work by reason of being postmaster.
The rate was in force when he took office.

The rate may have been too low. The hon. gentleman has been told by a zealous supporter of his own that these are growing times, that prices have increased, that the cost of living is greater and so on. If he pays any attention to it he knows perfectly well that the answer he gives in regard to that being the rate when he came into office is not a fair answer.
Mr. JOHNSTON (Cardwell.) I am pleased to know that I will be able to go back and tell the postmasters in my constituency that there is no hope held out by the hon. Postmaster General to them of an increase in their salaries. A few years ago when I spoke to the hon. Postmaster General, he said that he would give the subject his best consideration. He said that he was in favour of an increase and that he advocated it ?
I did not say that I advocated it.

The. hon. Postmaster General at least agreed in effect with what 1 said. Now, I can go back to the postmasters and tell them that the hon. Postmaster General says there is no relief for them. That is my understanding of the hon. gentleman's position. Notwithstanding that we heard him to-night declare in a braggadocio manner that he was increasing the salaries of the letter-carriers in the towns and cities, he refused to increase the salaries of postmasters in country places. These postmasters have to buy their own wood, they have to provide for themselves and the citizens who have to pay something out of their own pockets to get their papers.
Yet, the Postmaster General says there is no relief for them. Is that what I shall tell them, Mr. Postmaster General ? I am in earnest about it. I did tell them that the Postmaster General had said that he would give their case his most serious consideration, that he believed they had a grievance and that he would try to remedy it.
I think not.

I cannot quote the exact words, but that is the effect of the hon. gentleman's answer given to me a few years ago. I have had letters from some of the postmasters in my constituency asking me if they could not get some more remuneration for keeping the post office in the country, but I must now go back to them and say that the hon. Postmaster General holds no hope to them. They only get $20 for keeping a post office open, and if the stage comes along at seven o'clock in the morning they have to be up to see to tile mail and they have to continue, with perhaps some interruption, distributing letters until night. I think their request is a reasonable one and especiallv in view of the fact that the salaries of the letter-carriers and the salaries of ther officials have been raised. When you talk about the expense of living and the good times that we are having in this country, I think it is only fair that the salaries of these men should be raised to $50 for keeping a country post office. It would not cost any more to raise the salaries of the postmasters of the country to $50 a year, the amount they ask, than it would cost to raise the salaries of the letter-carriers in the cities. Some of the postmasters who are getting $20 would only require to have $30 added to their present salaries to make up the $50. To the salaries of others who are getting more you would have to add less, while, of course, to those who are getting $10 the increase would be greater. In .Caledon there is one man getting $20 and there is no other post office nearer than three and a half miles. For two and a half miles around the people come to the post office for their papers and the postmaster is on duty the whole day, handing out papers and only getting $20 a year for it. I leave it to the good sense of the House if it is fair to treat a man in that way.
Would the hon. gentleman give the name of that office ?
It is Sles-wick, between Caledon East and Mono Mills. There is another, Blount, in Mono.

I have listened with much interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Cardwell (Mr. Jolin-stjon).^ He very rarely trespasses on the time of the House and he always speaks with great earnestness. I tell him with all

frankness that I have the greatest respect for any view he may advance to this House,
I know he is most conscientious in the presentation of any case. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Johnston) must have misunderstood me if he thought I promised to deal with the subject. I may have expressed myself to the effect that these positions were rather nominal so far as salary goes, because these offices are established to accommodate very small groups of people, and more for the convenience of the neighbourhood than anything else. The postmaster of such an office as the hon. gentleman alludes to does not expect a substantial sum in the_ sense of salary. A small allowance having no reference to the time or labour involved is all he expects. It does not involve a man devoting himself to the post office ; as a rule it is carried on in a private house and some member of the family is always present. It will never be possible to remunerate people who keep post offices of that kind. For instance, I find from the report of the Postmaster General for the last iiscal year that the revenue of the Sleswick post office was $18.91. and that the postmaster was paid $20. The revenue represented only three letters a day posted at that office and therefore you will see that it serves only a very small group of people. But if it should happen that this post office has to be kept open at unreasonable hours because of the time of the arrival and the departure of the mails, this circumstance might be taken into consideration and the subject dealt with specifically, but it is one thing to deal with special cases and another thing to deal with the question generally. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Johnston) will be good enough to give me the facts connected with that particular case it will be looked into, and if I am not able to accede to his wishes it is not because I have not the greatest respect for anything he may say in this House.

I may say to the Postmaster General that a great many farmers get their papers at this post office, and as I said three years ago, Sleswick and other country post offices are great distributing offices but very poor receiving offices, because a great many people go to Mono Mills and Caldedon East and Charleston and buy their postage stamps there where they do their business, but they post their letters at Sleswick and consequently the revenue from the latter post office is comparatively very small. But there is a great deal of distributing to be done at the post office and a great deal of work to do. There are a great many other post offices in the same fix, and I hope that the postmaster at Sleswick will get something done for him. As the Postmaster General says some one has to be in the office all the time and there is not a holiday in the year that they can close the post office ; some one has to stay there and miss the enjoyment of the holiday.
Anything I can do to aid the postmaster to obtain fair remuneration I will be most willing to do it.

I do not for a moment seek to minimize the importance of the case which my hon. friend from Cardwell has been urging, but I do not agree with his suggestion that a certain amount should be cut from the pay of the town postmasters, in order to make up to the country postmasters. It is a poor proposition that an injustice should be perpetrated upon one class of the people for the sake of remedying the grievance of another class of the people. I can tell my hon. friend (Mr. Johnston) that so far as western Canada is concerned he is mistaken in thinking that the allowance given to the town postmasters is excessive. Since the commencement of this session the accounting postmasters, including the town postmasters of Manitoba and the North-west Territories, deemed it advisable to go to the expense of sending a delegation to Ottawa to present to the minister the grievances under which they labour. I know of one particular case where an allowance of $14 per month is paid to a town postmaster for rent, fuel, and light, and that postmaster is at present paying $25 per month for the premises he occupies as the post office, and which premises are only half the size that are required for that town. That is at Moosejaw.
What is the population ?
When the census was taken it was 2,000 and probably it would be 3,000 r ow.
It is a divisional point.

It is a railway divisional point, and quite an important place. The revenue from Moosejaw will be as large I suppose as that of a town of 7,000 or
8,000	or even 10,000 population. If the postmaster there was obliged to rent the building now I venture to say that he could not obtain it for less than $40 a month, and yet be is only allowed $14 a month for rental, fuel and light. I rose particularly to ask the Postmaster General if he has yet reached a decision with regard to the petition of the delegation that waited on him during the early weeks of the session to represent the interests of the town postmasters of Manitoba and the North-west Territories. The other day the Postmaster General told us when we were discussing his Bill relating to the increase of salaries of mail clerks, that he would consider certain matters if they were brought to his attention when the estimates were being discussed. I then complained of the insufficiency of the accommodation afforded by the mail' cars furnished by the railway companies. I stated that it had been found necessary to put the mails in box cars and

that sometimes on a train there would be a box car full of mail matter. As I stated the other day, the work of the mail clerks of the western division is rendered almost impossible.
There is another matter which, while on my feet, I would like to bring to the attention of the hon. Postmaster General. The appeals I have been making have been on behalf of a very limited number of people. I now wish to appeal on behalf of about
75.000	people who are served by the mail service on the Prince Albert branch railway. Last year I brought to the attention of the hon. Postmaster General the service on the Pasqua line, which forms a part of the Minneapolis, St. Paul and Sault Ste. Marie Railway, and I am very pleased to say that since that matter was sipoken of a step has been taken in the direction of giving a proper service to the country traversed by that line, by putting a mail car and a mail clerk on the railway. The same kind of service is very urgently required on the Prince Albert branch. At present the service is on the baggage car. There is no mail car and no mail clerk ; and when we recollect that that branch serves the whole Saskatchewan district^ which two years ago contained 26,000 people and must this year contain 60,000 people, and also a large portion of the district of Assiniboia, and it is not too much to say that
75.000	people are served by that branch line.

The hon. gentleman who has just sat down misunderstood me when he said that I recommended that the salaries of postmasters of cities and towns should be cut down. Two years ago I advocated increasing the remuneration of tlie country postmasters, and the Postmaster General asked me what I would propose. I said that if there was no other way of meeting their requirements, I would even go the length of taking something from the salaries of those who were getting from $1,500 to $2,000 a year and dividiug it among the postmasters in little country places. I did not say that that should be done, but I said that if the revenue of the country would not permit it to be done in any other way, I would resort to that.

The hon. member for Western Assiniboia has asked for an improved service bn the Prince Albert branch. The comptroller of the mail service informs me that until this year the trains on that branch were only running tri-weekly, and the mails could not be sent more frequently than that. But since there has been a daily train there has been a daily mail service. He informs me that no application has been made for any different service from the one now in existence.

I must inform the Postmaster General that the comptroller must 190
be mistaken, because months ago 1 wrote to the department applying for and recommending a mail car and mail clerk on this line.
To whom did you write ?

My recollection is that I wrote to the deputy minister, and since the commencement of this session I have had conversations with the comptroller about the matter, and I have again written on one or two occasions to the deputy minister to the same effect. It is quite true, as the Postmaster General states, that this spring the railway company put on a daily train, and a daily mail service has also been put on, for which the department is entitled to due credit. But the baggage car service is not sufficient for the large number of people served by that line.
The deputy informs me that he has not received any communication from the hon. gentleman.
Then there must be something radically wrong with the mail service, if my letters have not reached the deputy.

Is this the proper time to ask for information in regard to the disposition of the automobiles which were formerly used for the collection of mail matter from the letter boxes in the city of Toronto, and in regard to the contract which has been let for the collection of this matter, and also in regard to the conveyance of the mail to the station ?

The deputy informs me that the automobiles have not been dispensed with, but are still in use. But in some parts of the city they cannot be used owing to the state of the streets. They are used considerably for running between the branches and also between the post offices and the station. A contract was let this spring to a man named Power for collecting the mail matter from the letter boxes. It was let by public tender.
How many tenders were received ?
The deputy thinks four or five.
Were there advertisements calling for tenders ?
Yes.
Mr. Power was the lowest tenderer ?
He was.	,
Has the department to supply wagons ?
No, he is to supply wagons.
There were no wagons bought by the department ?
No.

I wish to call the attention of the hon. Postmaster General to the inefficiency of the postal seryice in the [DOT]county of Inverness, and to ask him if he has any encouragement to hold out of any improvement in that service ? I would like also to have some explanation of the attempted conversion of a daily service of some fifty miles into a tri-weekly service. The people of Inverness do not feel secure that some official may not take it into his head to dismantle the postal service in that county at any moment.

I will assure my hon. friend at once that I will never take into my head any such idea as that. I will attempt to give the county of Inverness the best service it is possible to give it, having due regard to the interests of the county and of the country generally. I will be able at a later stage to give the hon. gentleman all the information he desires on the subject he refers to. He correctly stated the other evening that I was absent from Canada at the time, and I cannot speak with any personal knowledge of the subject ; but, if I remember rightly, he heard of the proposed dismantling of the service from an officer on a train, and he immediately put himself in communication with the Finance Minister, who looked after his interests in the matter ; so that even if the postal service was insufficient, my hon. friend was fortunate in having the Finance Minister here to look after the interests of the county of Inverness. Although I was absent, I had an efficient colleague who saw that no injustice was done to the county of Inverness, and I can assure my hon. friend that I will be very careful to follow the lead he has set me.

I called the attention of the hon. Postmaster General the other evening to the insufficient postal service on the Inverness railway. I also did so last session and he gave me every assurance that he would look into th* matter. The service is somewhat akin to that referred to by the bon member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott). The mails are only taken on as baggage. They are taken through the county of Inverness, a distance of sixty-one miles, over the Inverness Railway, and through the county of Antigonisk on to the Intercolonial Railway, tliesce through Pic-tou county until they meet the east bound train for Sydney. The letters are then sorted by the mail clerks on the Intercolonial Railway mail car, taken back, and distributed along the Inverness Railway that evening or the next day. This I am thoroughly aware of and what no explanation of the officials can justify. We have good reason for complaint, and I only Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
hope that the hon. minister will mete out to the people of Inverness the same measure of justice that he has been pleased to give to the people of Assiniboia, in the instance of one railway which passes through that county. With regard to the other railways which go through Assiniboia, the hon. gentleman has promised to give the complaints his attention. All I ask is that the county of Inverness be similarly treated, as are those jieople who recently came into our western country. The people of Inverness have been residing there a long time, and are at least as much entitled to consideration as are the people who have come from every country in Europe into the Northwest in recent years. Let me also point out to the hon. gentleman that when the post office inspector of Nova Scotia went among the people of Inverness asking for tenders for a tri-weekly service for a distance of fifty miles, where formerly for thirty-five years there was a daily mail service, that matter was not at all so light and unimportant as the hon. the Postmaster General seems to view it, and the people really feel grateful to the hon. Minister of Finance who came to their rescue and will continue to feel under an obligation to him, as I certainly do.
What is the amount paid for the services rendered by Mr. Powell ?
I will have that on the supplementary estimates.
The Postmaster General has not stated what he intends doing for the county of Inverness.

My hon. friend asks me to do as well for the Inverness Railway as I have done for the Prince Albert branch. Well, it is given as good a service as is given on the Prince Albert branch. What the hon. gentleman really wishes is the establishment of a mail car on the railway.
Certainly.
That is what the hon. gentleman desires.
I desired it last year.

There are many things we desire which we cannot get. The establishment of a railway mail car service is somewhat expensive and cannot always be had. We must have some regard for the cost and the revenue and the district served. There are many places throughout Canada which have not postal car service. It has never been the practice of any government to establish indiscriminate postal car service, but to consider the merits of each application. I was speaking with the comptroller, and he informed me that he has the application of the county of Inverness under consideration. He is the expert officer who advises me with regard to

these matters, and I am sure he will be guided by the best interests of the country, and I hope that that will not conflict with the interests of the people of Inverness.

Some months ago, on the Wellington, Grey and Bruce branch of the Grand Trunk Railway, a fast train was put on connecting with Guelph and trains for the east, west and south, but there is no mail on that train which comes down in the evening. It would be a great convenience if it were given the mails, as it is one of the fastest trains on the road, and connects at Guelph with all the trains going east, west and south.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The discussion of the mail service is not in order on the item before the committee. We had better pass the first item.
I understood the hon. minister to say that the same allowances are given the country postmasters as were given by the previous government.
I said that we were dealing with them in the same scale. Whatever the scale was when I took office is in force to-day.

That would leave rather a false impression on the committee. You would naturally suppose that the country postmasters were receiving the same salaries to-day as under the former administration. But the hon. gentleman has told us that the revenue, in a large number of the smaller post offices, is less than it was before, because more post offices have been established, which necessitates a greater division of the revenue among them. That being the case, I suppose it is fair to assume that the average country postmaster is receiving less now than he did under the former administration.

My officers inform me that that is not correct. There are fluctuations in salaries as there are in revenues, but some salaries are fixed. Where the salary is in proportion to the revenue, that is where it is paid by a commission, there is fluctuation, but there has been no reduction of revenue because of any reduction in the rate of postage.

I see that the comptroller of the railway mail service is here, and I wish to call his attention to the fact that the hon. the Postmaster General has reduced the cost of the mail service in the county of Inverness by over 55,000 a year for the last seven years. That would amount to something like $35,000. When the comptroller is called upon to make a report with regard to putting a mail clerk on board that train I hope he will take into consideration the fact that $35,000 has been sweated out of that service in the past seven years.
190}	.

I confess that I do not follow the statement made by the hon. Postmaster General with respect to the salaries of country postmasters. I am anxious to get the information and have no other object. Am I to understand that the salaries of postmasters do not increase with the revenue of their jjoat offices ? Or, if that is not a correct statement, will the hon. gentleman give us an illustration of how the sliding scale he speaks of applies to a country district like his own county ?

The scale of payment to the postmasters paid by way of commissions^ is as follows : 40 per cent upon the gross revenue up to $800, 25 per cent on the excess between $800 and $10,000; 15 per cent on the excess over $10,000.
If the revenue is $150, do I understand the Postmaster General to say the postmasters receives 40 per cent on that amount ?
Yes.
The hon. gentleman's (Hon. Sir William Mulock) report does not appear to bear that out, as he will see by referring to the case of almost any country post office.
The accountant of the department tells me that that is lived up to.
Would the hon. minister turn to the case referred to by the hon. member for Cardwell, that of Sleswick.

I except from that, offices where there is a fixed salary. In the case of Sleswick, the postmaster is paid a fixed salary of $20. The gross revenue there is $18. In these small, minor offices, the rule does not apply. Forty per cent on $1 would be only $7.20. Therefore the rule does not apply.
The hon. minister's statement was misleading, therefore I did not understand him. He makes the statement that up to $800 the postmasters are paid, by commission.
I qualified that.

Then, the fact is that the Postmaster General was not discussiug the underpaid postmasters whose cases the committee ane trying to understand. Will he tell us what is the policy of the government with regard to the payment of postmasters where the revenue runs from $18 up to $50 ?
The accountant informs me that where the revenue is $30 or under, the 40 per cent does not apply, because it would give the posh master less than is desirable; but, above $sfe I the scale is applied.
Then, do I understand that if the revenue of the post office is $40 the salary of the postmasters is $10 V If that statement is correct then the hon. gentleman's report is not correct.

In the case of a small office, where the salary has been fixed in years gone by, that salary has not been lowered even where the revenue has fallen. Therefore, the hon. gentleman will find many eases of postmasters receiving a fixed sum which is far in excess of 40 per cent of the revenue. These fixed fees have been handed down to us by our predecessors.
Here is an office the revenue of which is $36, in a country district in the province of Ontario. According to the hon. minister's scale, what payment would the postmaster receive ?

If he is paid by a percentage, it would be 40 per cent of the revenue, and the hon. gentleman ([DOT]Mr. Blain) can compute that. But, it may be that the salary was fixed at some anterior time and has not been disturbed.
Then, the hon. gentleman's statement with respect to 40 per cent does not hold good there ?
What is the office ?
I find it at page 35 of the Postmaster General's Report. Take any of the offices there. The one I was referring to was Dunkeld in the country of Bruce.
The postmaster is paid $20.

What is the scale of revenue in a case like that ? They vary in every page of this report. The hon. minister must not misunderstand my desire; all I want is to know what the policy of the department is with respect to the payment of postmasters in country districts where the revenue runs from $40 to $150. Is there any fixed policy ?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) asks about a case like; Dunkeld which has a revenue of $36 and the postmaster is paid $20. The officers of the department explained to me that that $20 was evidently paid soihe years ago, probably when the revenue was higher. It may have fallen because of some other offices being opened near it, or for some other cause, but the department has not lowered his salary. But if this were an office to be opened in the first instance today, the scale would apply. We do not, however, apply the scale to reduce the salaries which we found in existence.
Then, the fact is that where a country postmaster received $20 in former days, he receives the same salary now.

That is the rule.
Mr. BLAIN The post office at Dunlop in the county of Gloucester, has a revenue of $34.75. Can the hon. gentleman tell us, according to his scale, what the postmaster would receive in that case ? He says the postmasters are paid a percentage when the revenue is above $30.
According to the scale it would be 40 per cent.
The policy of the government is what I want to get at. Where the revenue of the post office is $34.75, what is the policy the hon. gentleman applies to the payment of the postmasters ?

I have answered that question several times. The policy of the department is to pay the postmaster aeording to a certain scale. Where the revenue is small and a fixed allowance is made, the commission system of remuneration does not apply, but in other cases it does apply, and then the postmasters are paid a commission according to the volume of the revenue, subject to the qualification which I made some time ago that we do not, and have not, reduced any salaries based upon a commission where the reduction of revenue was in consequence of a reduction of the rate of postage.

The hon. gentleman says that the postmasters are paid according to the revenue in towns of 2,000 or 3,000 inhabitants. In Ridgetown, where the revenue is $3,496, the salary is $1,000. In Morrisburg, where the revenue is $3,202, the salary is $1,000. It cannot therefore be on a fixed percentage that these two salaries are paid.

The accountant informs me that the amount of salary is based upon the revenue of the preceding year. For example we are now in the month of July, the fiscal year closes the 30th June, in a short time the revenue from the post offices of Canada will be ascertained, and then the department will fix the salaries for the current year according to the revenue up to the 30th of June last. I do not know from what year the hon. gentleman takes his figures.

Well, the salary commencing on the first day of July, 1902. was based upon the revenue for the fiscal year that closed on the 30th of June, 1902. So the hon. gentleman will have to take the report of the previous year. The accountant informs me that the same rule applies to all.

Then the revenues of these pest offices were a year ago exactly the same, but the figures do not show it. For the information of the Postmaster General,

I will refer to the town of Preston, where the revenue is $3,907, or $700 more than in Morrisburg, and the salary is $950, while in Morrisburg the salary is $1,000. I will take Newmarket, where the revenue of the post office is $3,405, and the salary is $985. At Mount Forest, the revenue is $3,567 and the salary $1,120. I hope the statement of the Postmaster General that the salaries are based upon a percentage will be carried out. But I cannot see how the salaries in Ridge-tcwn and Morrisburg should be exactly the same where the revenues are not the same.
Is the hon. gentleman quoting figures for the present year or the preceding year 7
For the preceding year.
Then the figures are not the figures upon which the salaries at the present moment are based.

When we look at the allowances paid to postmasters, I find that at Morrisburg the salary and allowances are $1,573, where the revenue is $3,200 : While in Preston, w ith a revenue of nearly $4,000, the salary and allowances are $1,208.

I cannot to-night explain the figures of the department in regard to these post offices. But the accountant who is present informs me that the rule I have quoted several times is applied. If the hon. gentleman desires any information with regard to revenue of salaries in any office, he wall be furnished it, the department wrill endeavour to satisfy the hon. gentleman. I never interfere with the salaries paid to postmasters. Changes are made automatically by the department, and each postmaster is entitled to his rights, and if he does not get them it is certainly r.ot my fault.
I suppose the Postmaster General will see to it that if the postmaster at Preston does not get his salary according to the percentage, he will be paid the amount due him for past services.
Certainly, and every one else.

I would like
to ask the hon. Postmaster General if the vacancy at Chatsworth has been filled and if so by whom ?
I cannot give the hon. gentleman the name, but I understand there has been an appointment.

I understand that Mr. Macdonald of Chatsworth, a local banker, was appointed to that position. The hon. Postmaster General visited that district during the by-election and the result of it was that a promise which had been given by the late representative (Dr. Horsey), was not carried out. The late Dr. Horsey promised that appointment to Mr. Dobie. It is to be regretted that his wishes were not carried out in this matter. It seems to be a matter of the basest ingratitude on the part of the Liberal party and I say that the least the hon. Postmaster General could have done was to carry out the wishes of the late Dr. Horsey in this matter.

I want to ask the hon. Postmaster General how it comes that where an office, Dwight, in the Muskoka and Parry Sound district, has a revenue of $130, the salary of the postmaster is $50, while at another office, Dyment, Algoma, which has a revenue of $129, the salary is $70. This is a matter that requires some explanation so that we will be able to understand how these salaries are fixed.
I will have the information for the hon. gentleman.

I, would like to ask the hon. Postmaster General if any letter-carriers are employed in Prince Edward Island. We have Charlottetown with a population of 12,000 and Summerside with a population of 4,000, and there is no mail delivery outside of the general post office.

It has not been the practice to establish the letter-carrier system generally throughout Canada in all cities and towns, and there has been no fixed rule upon this subject, but I fancy the practice has been to adopt the system in the leading cities. Of course, I would not underestimate the importance of Charlottetown. It is the largest city in the province of Prince Edward Island. At the same time, compared with other centres of population throughout the Dominion, there are many much more populous than Charlottetown that have not yet had the benefit of the letter-carrier system. I did not find when I took office that the late government had favourably dealt with the case of Charlottetown. I did not find that they were prepared to establish the letter-carrier system at Charlottetown, and I have not yet been able to take exception to that view. I hope, however, that Charlottetown will grow in importance, wealth and population and win for itself the distinction of having a free letter delivery system established there.

I am very much pleased to get the explanation of the hon. Postmaster General and I am in hopes that Charlottetown will grow in importance. But, the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) spoke the other day in favour of a rural distribution of mails and I would suppose that a city like Charlottetown, having a population of 12,000 or 13,000, would be entitled to some advantage in that respect. The hon. Postmaster General received a

letter from me a few days ago in regard to the post office at Portage on the line of the Prince Edward Island Railway. Has the hon. gentleman considered that matter ?
The practice would be that the letter would be forwarded to the inspector on the island to make his report. I suppose it has not yet been received.

I desire also to call the attention of the hon. Postmaster General to another matter in regard to a place called lot 14, in Prince county, where there is a semi-weekly mail and where the people are now very anxious to have a daily mail. This is quite an important village. They have lately established a cheese factory and as other matters in connection with the business of the country are progressing they ask that this semi-weekly mail should be superseded by a daily mail. I trust the hon. minister will take into consideration the requirements of that part of the country. He should only have to ask his inspector down there in regard to the propriety of having this request earned out and that gentleman would say that in consequence of the establishments there that the farmers require this further accommodation for the purpose of carrying on their affairs.

Has there been a formal application made to the department as to this increased mail service ? If there has been such an application it will go to the inspector and be reported on, then his report will come to the department, will be considered, and if the report shows the service should be increased it will be increased, but if it does not show that I am afraid it will not be increased. We have to depend upon the case presented by the inspector.

I have always found the hon. minister on the report of his inspector to act fairly by the people, and although I cannot say positively, I am pretty sure that the inspector will report in favour of the increased accommodation. I have always found that when a good prima facie case was made out the hon. Postmaster General was likely to fall in with what was suggested.

I do not think the Postmaster General has given all the information in connection with this appointment at Chatsworth. I think he must have some knowledge of the appointment, because he was there during the by-election, and no doubt talked it over. If the appointment was not made by him, I would like to know who recommended the appointment. These are simple questions that should be answered.

It is not the practice to inform the House on Mr. HACKETT.
whose nomination any one is appointed. The minister takes the responsibility. If there has been an appointment made at Chatsworth I take the responsibility of that appointment, and I have made it on what I deemed proper authority. More than that I am not able to say.

In the county which I have the honour to represent there are three postmasters, one of whom has been keeping the post office for thirty-three years, another one for twenty-six years, and another for twenty years. Before I left home in March these three gentlemen came to me and asked me to request the Postmaster General if he will allow them for house rent.
What are the names please ?

I will give the names a little later on. They see an item in the estimates for rent of post offices, and they think they should be allowed rent for their post offices. They are not very extravagant people and they would be satisfied with $12 a year each. They do not claim any back rent, but they believe that if the government pays rent for post offices elsewhere, they should have an allowance for rent. In the town in which I live the post office has been opened for fifty years and the present postmaster has been in charge for thirty-three years. A little bit of a scale has been sent to the postmaster that is of no use at all, and it is not suitable for the requirements of the office. Now I think the Postmaster General should send a scale to that postmaster. He cannot weigh five pounds of mail matter on a scale that will only fit one pound. If the Postmaster General-wishes, I will go to the Post Office Department and tell the deputy the names of the postmasters who asked for an increase.
Yery well. The deputy informs me that the postmasters are entitled to a set of scales equal to the requirements of the office.
What was the value of the issue of the so called jubilee stamps, and what was the highest denomination I
It is six years ago since they were issued, and I cannot exactly say what the issue was, but the highest denomination was $5.

It is a matter of general complaint throughout the country that a large number of these so called jubilee stamps are now repudiated by the government. That is serious when you come to think that some of them have a denomination of $5. When the issue was placed upon the market a great number of children were induced to buy them, and as a consequence some of these stamps are yet held by people

throughout the country. It is due to the holders of these stamps that an order should immediately be issued by the department that one cent or two cent stamps should be exchanged in return for these stamps of large denomination. It is not creditable to a great country like this that it should issue stamps and then repudiate them. If they are not exchanged, a great deal of loss and inconvenience will be suffered by a great many people. What does the Postmaster General propose to do ?

There is ample occasion of making use of these stamps in Canada. It is not necessary to affix them to a letter. There are many ways in which postage far in excess of $5 can be paid. There is no country in the world that redeems postage stamps. When postage stamps are issued they are issued for good. Occasionally when there has been a fire in a post office, or where by some accident a large quantity of stamps become soiled and useless, we have substituted others for them. There is a large amount of mail matter mailed in Canada and posted in bulk ; there is not a particular stamp fixed to each piece of mail matter, but the payment is made on the bulk amount. For example, take a news ageit who is sending out magazines in great quantities. There is no separate postage stamp put on each separate piece, but the payment is made in bulk. The Toronto post office receives daily large sums, sometimes in money, sometimes in postage, and these stamps are just as goods as any other stamps.

' I find, on reference to the Postmaster General's report, that there *was on hand at the beginning of this year $30,680 worth of Jubilee stamps, and that there was on hand at the close of the year $30,680 worth. In other words, there was not a buyer in the whole Dominion for one of these stamps. This goes to show that people know that these stamps are practically worthless unless they can be converted into stamps of lower denominations. I cannot understand where it would be possible, in the ordinary course of trade, for people to require a $5 stamp, and there is the fact standing plain that the department have been utterly unable to sell any of these stamps. May I ask, does the department hand out these stamps as it does current and negotiable stamps ?

The deputy informs me that the value the hon. gentleman refers to of these high denominations has been reduced by over $7,000, to some $23,000 at the present time. I repeat that the stamps are available, there is a legitimate demand for them, and all any one requires to do with these stamps, if he does not want to use them, is to transmit them where they will be used. I have not any doubt that if any person wants to exchange
these stamps for stamps of smaller denominations, the department will accede to his request.
Then, do I understand that any person applying to the department at Ottawa will have smaller stamps issued in exchange for $5 stamps or other stamps of large denomination ?

I do not say that it would be done at any post office. It might inconvenience the postmaster by depriving him of the necessary supply of stamps for the ordinary use of customers; but if transmitted to the head office here, the exchange would readily be made.

I would like to ask the hon. Postmaster General about the establishment of a branch post office in the northern part of the town of Barrie. In speaking of this, it will be recognized that I am speaking of something in a constituency which I do not represent. However, I am speaking with the consent of the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy) to whom I spoke about the matter to-night. About a year ago I was requested to prepare a petition for this post office. I did so, and it was numerously signed. The matter was inaugurated, I think, by a gentleman named Sproatt. The post office would be available to a large number of people in the northern part of the town of Barrie, and in the country roundabout, who cannot be very well served by the post office at Barrie. It is pointed out that a place could be got for the post office on the line of the mail route between Barrie and Midhurst, and that it would be a great convenience to a large section of the country as well as a considerable section of the town, and I do not know that it would entail any expense on the Post Office Department.

The petition which the hon. gentleman has spoken of was forwarded by him through me to the Postmaster and was urged upon the Postmaster General by me for his consideration. I received a reply, which I communicated to my hon. friend, that it would receive the consideration of the Postmaster General. I do not think the situation of the post office is quite correctly stated by my hon. friend. I do not think it is in the limits of the town of Barrie, but outside the limits. It was to be called Yespra, after the name of the township in which it would be situated. Mr. Sproatt lives outside the limits of the town of Barrie, about a mile and a half from the town, on the line between Midhurst and Barrie, which has a daily mail service. A mail bag could easily be left off at Mr. Sproatt's house. This would be of advantage to a section of the community. That was pointed out to the department by me. But I recognize that if

a post office is opened there it should be on the distinct understanding that the postmaster would be willing to accept the remuneration which the department ordinarily allows, and would not encourage any demand for more pay. Upon that understanding, I would urge the hon. Postmaster General to grant the request.

My hon. friend from North Simcoe is probably correct in saying that the post office will be established in Yespra. At the same time, it would serve a number of people in the northern part of Barrie as well as many people in the township of Yespra. There is a schoolhouse in the immediate neighbourhood, and children from two or three miles around, in a thickly settled part of Yespra, would come there and be able to take the mail to the people in the evening. In what my hon. friend says as to the remuneration of the postmaster, I am not very much concerned. I presume that it would not be on the basis of percentage if the revenue is exceedingly small, but that the hon. Postmaster General would make it on as generous a basis as those spoken of to-night, where the revenue is only $30 or $40, while the remuneration is $20. If the hon. the Postmaster General will take the matter into consideration and establish a post office, I am sure there will be no difficulty on the score of remuneration. Mr. Sproat is a supporter of the Liberal party, and I have no doubt will be very reasonable in his views and is prepared to accept what is fair under the circumstances.

This case seems to be very well supported on both sides, and I am glad to find there is something on which both sides can agree. I cannot promise anything further than that the matter will receive careful consideration.
There will be no extra expense involved because the postmasters are paid according to the revenue.
How will it be served ?
By the same carrier as now brings the mails. You would have to give him some nominal remuneration.

The remarks of my hon. friend from West Prince concerning the mail delivery at Charlottetown were very timely and I did not hear the hon. the Postmaster General give any good reason why the city of Charlottetown should be without letter-carriers. I should like to know on what principle he grants the different towns these letter-carriers. I find that there are towns in Ontario with much smaller population which have the advantage of this service.

Where are they ?
Mr. McCarthy.

There is the town of Barrie, with a population of about 6,000 and a revenue of some $9,000, while Charlottetown has over 13,000 population and a revenue of over $17,600. I cannot see why Charlottetown should not be served as well as some of the smaller towns in Ontario.
The hon. member for West Prince brought the matter up earlier in the evening and I then gave my views on the subject and I have nothing to add to what I then said.

I do not consider that the hon. minister gave any very good answer for my hon. friend from West Prince. He said that the matter was under consideration at one time, but nothing was done. That was not laying down the principle on which he gives letter-carriers to the different towns throughout the Dominion. There must be some principle, either on the basis of population or revenue.

As regards the town of Barrie, I am told that some twenty years ago a letter-carrier was appointed for that place by the late Conservative government. I do not know why they slighted Charlottetown. Perhaps my hon. friend could find that out. I myself did not establish the system at Barrie, but have not disturbed it. My impression is that it was to meet some special case, and I only learned by accident that there was a letter-carrier there.

We are not dealing with the past, but the future, I would like to know why the hon. gentleman himself neglected Charlottetown as he has done for the last seven years. The people there deserve equal treatment witli the people of Ontario and the rest of the Dominion, and I should like to know what the hon. minister proposes to do in the future.

When the city of Charlottetown requests the department to establish a letter-carrier system or do anything else in connection with the mail service, that application will receive careful consideration.
I am very glad that I have at last got the principle upon which the minister conducts the business of his department. You have simply to make application and you will get what you apply for.

Ask and you shall receive.
Mr. LEFURGEYL There is just one other matter to which I wish to refer. That is the case of Kelley's Cross. I pointed out, last night that the people in that locality were at a great disadvantage. It takes from twenty-four to thirty-six hours to carry their mails a distance of eighteen miles.

While Kelley's Cross gave a revenue of 1)167.25, and the postmaster there was paid $24, as the hon. minister pointed out last night, he left out of consideration the fact that there are four other post offices, whose revenue should have been taken into account, and among those five post offices the revenue amounts to .$246, and the expenses to $100, leaving a balance of $146 to the good. From Kelley's Cross to New Wiltshire, the amount of $125 which the hon. minister gave us last year, was for the carrying of the mails between these two places and taking in also Elm Yale and Bookval. What the people want is to have the mails carried from New Wiltshire to the railway station, which is only a matter of some three quarters of a mile and costs $35. So that the expense of the service would simply be doubling the $35 and not doubling the $125.
Mail service, $2,382,850.
What does that include?
That includes the land service, amounts paid to contractors by land, rail service, courier and on foot.
May I ask if the same form of contract for mail carriers in rural districts is in use now was in use under the former administration ?
The deputy informs me that it is very much the same. There have been some slight changes.
Would the minister kindly tell us what those changes are ?
I could not without comparison of the two contracts. The deputy tells me that some vagueness was removed.
I am informed that a percentage was taken off
I know what the hon. gentleman refers to.
Then, would the hon. gentleman be good enough to give us the information ?

I do not know if we could say it was taken off, unless you count it as being added in the first instance. Contractors leave one per cent of the contract price in the hands of the government as an insurance fund. It frequently happens that contractors break down or fail to perform their contract or otherwise refuse, and, in order to have our accounts so that we can depend upon them, we have this special fund. Just as we have another fund for the insurance of the fidelity of the staff. We have a numerous staff, and, in order to save them being obliged to apply to their friends for bonds or to go to guarantee companies there is a small
charge against them, and that is put into the fund. The fund is made up from these two sources, contributions are on the assessment system.
Does that apply to country carriers ?
Yes, it is advertised.
Is this in place of the sureties that were asked for formerly ?
No, that is an assurance not only upon the contractor, but also upon his surety.

Then, if the country mail-carrier was to receive $125 per year for carrying mail under the former administva-tion, he was paid the full amount quarterly. But under the present administration, a percentage is taken off ?
No, that is not correct.
Then, will the minister please explain ?

When a service is let it is set forth in the advertisement that one per cent of the contract will be retained by the department for the purpose I have named. That one per cent becomes the property of the Crown and goes into this fund. The contractor takes that into consideration when he makes up his tender.

When the mails are carried across the straits and landed on Prince Edward Island what facilities are there for carrying them to their destination? Does the hon. minister intend to do in the future what he has done in the past and allow the mails to remain at Cape Traverse or Georgetown for hours waiting for the regular train.
The mails are conveyed by train from Cane Traverse and Georgetown-the train goes down to the dock.
Last year, the mails were delayed for hours at Georgetown, Summer-side and Cape Traverse, because the government would not pay for a train to carry them.
That is all over now, that is all settled.

Now, I would like to ask the minister vvliat information the hon. member for King's had in connection with this matter ?

I presume the hon. member for King's made the statement on the information he received from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries iHon. Mr. Prefontaine), and as the lion. Minister of Marine and Fisheries is not here I cannot ascertain the facts. If the hon. member (Mr. Hackett) will leave the question in my hands, I will get him the information.

On the question we were discussing before the hon. member for West Prince (Mr. Hackett) rose, I wish to ask one other question. Do I understand the hon. minister to say that when he puts an advertisement in the newspapers calling for tenders for the carrying of the mail between the two points, he states in that advertisement that one per cent will be deducted ?

It is not the practice to advertise all the specifications but to deposit a copy with the postmaster and at other places for the convenience of contemplating tenderers, and the advertisement informs the public where the form of contract may be seen. If the would-be-tenderer goes to the post office as he would have to do to get a form of tender he would have an opportunity of seeing the form of contract. I do not know that it is stated in the tender, but the tenderer lias an opportunity of knowing the facts.
Do I understand the Postmaster General to say that, notwithstanding the deducting of one per cent the maii-carrier has still to give bonds for the performance of his contract the same as before V
I stated that.
Then, I do not quite understand what the one per cent is for.
To insure the surety as well as the contractor.

For illustration, here is a man who carried the mail between two points ten miles apart for the former administration. When he signed the contract he was asked to give bonds for the carrying out of the contract. The bondsmen were his securities to the government. Under the new arrangement the mail-carrier is asked to pay one per cent of the contract price, and he still has to give the same bonds to the government. The fact is that the mail-carrier is made to pay and is not relieved at all of the amount of bonds he has to give for the performance of his contract. Now, what position would the mail-carrier have to take in order that the department might receive from this fund some advantage ?
Would he have to be an absconder, or be a man who did not fulfil his contract ? What wrong would he have to commit in order that something would be paid out of the fund that has accumulated under the one per cent deduction ?

If the mail contractor should, for any reason, cease to perform his contract and there was a difficulty in securing its performance by the sureties, the department would proceed to get the service performed in some other way, and if there was any loss, then it would have recourse to this fund to make good the loss.
And in the contract that he signs, it is stated at one per cent ?
Yes.

I want to draw the attention of the minister to a statement that appeared in the Toronto ' Star ' some time ago respecting the method that was to be adopted by the department in furnishing supplies for the post office. The Toronto ' Star ' is a paper very friendly to the hon. gentleman. Under the big heading ' Current wages and union hours-the stipulations for all who furnish post office supplies,' I find this item, dated Ottawa, August 28 :
Hon. William Mulock has decided that all men or firms furnishing supplies of all kinds to the Post Office Department must pay the current rate of wages to their employees and adopt the union hours of labour. This applies to goods whether sold under contract or not. At present the regulations apply only to contracts, but the principle has now been extended so as to become operative in the case of all who are on the patronage list of the department. Hereafter all persons who sell goods to the Post Office Department will have to make a sworn declaration that they have complied with the new regulation before they will receive payment.
I propose, when this matter is brought up further, to ask the hon. gentleman for a copy of the sworn declaration referred to, and also for an explanation as to what is meant by this despatch, whether it is correct or not, and if this regulation is well enforced.
If the hon. gentleman will let me have the article, I will see that the Information is obtained, and will produce a copy of the affidavit.
And the names of those who are on the patronage list ?
I may be able to give that information as well, hut I will not make any promise.

I understand the hon. gentleman is willing, provided that these items ' Miscellaneous and Yukon Territory ' are allowed to pass, that when his estimates come up again the subjects may he fully gone into and discussed.
Yes, everything in my department, inside and outside, may be discussed.
